speechtext: REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "NEW CANADIAN" OF FEBRUARY 28-FURTHER COMMENT IN "news herald"

Mr. Speaker, I again rise to a question of privilege. On Friday last when the house opened I took occasion to rise to a question of privilege in connection with an article which had appeared in a Japanese-owned and printed newspaper in Vancouver, wherein certain remarks were made concerning myself.
I am in receipt this morning of an article sent to me by air mail. This article appeared in the Vancouver News Herald of March 15, and under the heading "Reid Claims B.C. Members Make 'Malicious' Attack," it states:
Tom Reid (Liberal, New Westminster) issued a blanket charge in the House of Commons esterday that fellow British Columbia mem-ers had made a "false, malicious" attack on him.
The article continues:
Refers to Green.
Reid said that he was referring especially to Howard Green (Conservative, Vancouver South) and Angus Maclnnis (C.C.F., Vancouver East). He declared their attack had been over the Japanese problem in the Pacific province.
"I have never tried to raise hostile or racial hostile feeling against the Japanese," he said. "I merely tried to point out at times the dangers of giving the Japanese the franchise."
Whether the Nipponese were Canadian born or not, Reid declared, they owed their first loyalty to Tokyo, not to the dominion.
In fairness to the hon. members and in fairness to myself I believe some correction should be made, because when I spoke on Friday last I made no reference slightingly to any hon. member. I was dealing particularly with an article printed and directed against myself, which had appeared in the New Canadian, a paper issued by the Japanese of Vancouver.

ROYAL CANADIAN AIR FORCE-COMMISSIONING OF OFFICERS
speechtext:
1.	On completing a course of training in the R.C.A.F., what basis is followed in granting commissions and sergeant's rank?
2.	What standard of examination is required for these various ranks?
3.	Who is responsible for these appointments?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN AIR FORCE-COMMISSIONING OF OFFICERS
speechtext:
It is presumed that this
question refers to aircrew trained under the British commonwealth air training plan.
1.	Approximately 50 per cent of the aircrew trained as pilots or air observers are to be commissioned. Approximately 33 per cent are awarded on graduation and 17 per cent awarded for service in the field. The remainder of the aircrew trainees who complete their training are promoted to the rank of sergeant on graduation.
2.	The standard of examinations on completion of the course is in accordance with the syllabus of training as approved by the air ministry. The examinations consist of:
Ground subjects-These include navigation, signalling, airmanship, ground gunnery and the theory of bombing.
Flying training-Consisting of aerobatics, forced landing, service manoeuvres of aircraft in the air, air gunnery and practice bombing.
Officer qualities-An assessment made by the instructors during the course of training, considering capabilities as to leadership, initiative, educational background and deportment. The assessments in the above phases of training determine the degree of efficiency of all trainees and is the basis of selection for commissioning.
3.	The process of making the appointments to commissioned rank begins at the school where a board of officers is formed to recommend 50 per cent of each class for appointment to commissioned rank. This board submits their recommendations in order of priority
Questions

for the whole class. The recommendations are forwarded to the air officer commanding the command in which the school is located and he in turn submits to air force headquarters his recommendations for appointment to commissioned rank. Appointments to commissioned rank are made under the authority of the Minister of National Defence for Air. The minister's appointments are made on recommendations of a selection committee, presided over by a wing commander of the Royal Canadian Air Force and composed of representatives of the R.A.F., R.A.A.F., R.N.Z.A.F. and the R.C.A.F. All appointments made in the services of the commonwealths other than Canada are, of course, subject to their respective governmental approval.

subtopic: ARRIVAL IN CANADA OP CERTAIN BRITISH OFFICIALS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ARRIVAL IN CANADA OP CERTAIN BRITISH OFFICIALS
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the
Postal Censorship

Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock), and I should like to preface it by saying that if a reply is not considered in the public interest I will accept that explanation. Some six weeks ago there appeared a press notice to the effect that twenty-four officials had come from Great Britain and taken up residence in Vancouver to perform certain duties in connection with postal work in that city. My question is whether these officials are here at the request of the postal authorities of Canada, and what special work is required of them.

subtopic: ARRIVAL IN CANADA OP CERTAIN BRITISH OFFICIALS
speechtext:
The hon. member was kind enough to give me notice of his question. In reply I would say that he is correct in stating that approximately twenty-four men and women were sent from England to Canada in connection with censorship work. I would advise the hon. member that the facts in connection with this matter are as follows.
Representatives of the British government, including the director of imperial censorship, interviewed me and gave me certain information of a confidential nature which I do not consider it to be in the public interest to disclose at this time. I will say, however, that for reasons given to me at that time I agreed that Great Britain should send these people to Canada to do certain highly specialized censorship work. I feel that it is the duty of my department and myself as minister to cooperate to the fullest possible extent with the British authorities in this vital war work, while safeguarding the interests of our people in Canada. I was informed at the time the arrangements were made, and I have since been advised by officials of my department, that the people referred to in the hon. member's question have certain training, experience and qualifications for a special kind of work, and their duties are not merely those of translators or supervising translators.
Although the hon. member did not specifically ask, I think he would be interested to know that while in Canada these censors are under the control and direction of the chief postal censor of Canada, and that the expense of sending them to Canada was borne entirely by the British government. Further, although payment of their salaries is provided for in a vote under censorship in the war appropriations of the Post Office Department, the arrangement is that these moneys are repayable by the British government, who are responsible for the payment of their salaries, their respective rates of pay, and any allowances they may receive. Their employment in Canada has in no way affected the employment of Canadians for Canadian postal censorship work.

speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) if any representations have been made to the government of British Columbia offering assistance in the matter of freight rates on feed grains, similar to the assistance that has been offered other provinces.

I have heard it suggested in this house that it is sometimes dangerous to make predictions; perhaps it would be well, therefore, if I did not endeavour to mention a definite date. I can assure the hon. member for Peel, however, that the necessary machinery is being put into operation as fast, I believe, as is possible to ensure the very earliest possible application of the act.
There is one difficulty which I know the house will appreciate, namely, that the plan has to be one hundred per cent complete
before it is put into operation. It is not something that you can develop at one point and then spread it to another. In other words, before operation of the act commences the whole plan must be completely organized and ready to start as a completed task; it is not one that can be gradually developed. I can assure the hon. member that no steps are being left untaken to ensure that the act will come into operation at the earliest possible moment.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO QUESTIONING AND INVESTIGATION OF TWO JOUBNALISTS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO QUESTIONING AND INVESTIGATION OF TWO JOUBNALISTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the last sitting of the house on Friday the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) asked me to make a statement on a certain matter to which he called my attention. I quote his words, from page 1539 of Hansard:
I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to an article in this week's Saturday Night, which just by chance relates to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and their activities, for which body I have the greatest respect. This article purports to have been written in reply to certain statements made in this house by the minister on March 4. In the article it is categorically stated that two journalists, whose loyalty is unquestioned, namely Miss Judith Robinson and Mr. Oakley Dalgleish, have been questioned and investigated by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It is suggested in the article that the purpose of this questioning and investigation was to intimidate these journalists who have been critical of this government's war effort. The freedom of the
?ress is a matter of such vital importance that believe this house is entitled to a full and complete explanation from the minister.
Complying with the request of my hon. friend, I desire to make this statement.
In the issue of March 1 of the Toronto Saturday Night an article appeared by "Politicus", in which is stated:
Politicus knows of two cases of newspaper people of the highest loyalty and integrity whom the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are investigating and on whom they have a dossier. And in neither of these cases, both journalists being people whom Politicus knows well, is there the slightest doubt of their anxiety, perhaps over-anxiety, if there can be such a thing, for Britain to win this war, and of their responsibility.
On Tuesday, March 4, I stated in the House of Commons, in effect, that the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had advised me that such statement was incorrect.

In the issue of March 15 of Toronto Saturday Night, "Politicus" again refers to this matter and names the two persons to whom he had reference in his article on March 1 as Miss Judith Robinson and Mr. Oakley Dalgleish, and gives certain information which indicates that these two parties were interviewed by a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police particularly for the purpose of obtaining the name of the printers who printed certain posters in connection with the "Calling Canada Campaign".
On the 6th June, 1940, the commissioner received a poster called "Tanks or King, You Can't Have Both", together with a request that information be obtained as to the parties responsible for the publication or printing of the document, there being nothing on the poster indicating such information.
On the 27th June, 1940, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin)-asked a question in the house respecting "Calling Canada" advertisements, and I replied, as reported at page 1183 of Hansard, in effect that I was submitting the matter to the law officers and to the Secretary of State.
On the 2nd July, 1940, this matter was raised in the house by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) and I replied, as reported at page 1245 of Hansard, in effect, after quoting a telegram I had received from Judith Robinson, Oakley Dalgleish and J. R. Robinson, reading as follows:
Understand you wish to investigate our organization "Calling Canada". We are at room 264 Chateau Laurier.-
that it was not my purpose to investigate these highly estimable persons, and repeated, in part, what I stated on the 27th June.
The police, as a result of the request of the 6th June, 1940, for information, made an investigation. This was carried on under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police file heading of "Poster-Tanks or King, You Can't Have Both", and all information obtained in respect to such investigation is contained in that file.
The commissioner advises that there was no investigation made of Miss Robinson or Mr. Dalgleish, nor is there any individual or personal file or dossier in the police records respecting either of these two persons. The investigation respecting the poster was completed on or about the 23rd August, 1940, and no further inquiries have been made.
Miss Robinson and Mr. Dalgleish, contrary to the statement in the Toronto Saturday Night "that they have both been repeatedly and excessively 'quizzed' by an officer of the R.C.M.P." were each, in fact, interviewed in connection with this matter on only one occasion.

Debert Military Camp
The loyalty and integrity of Miss Robinson and Mr. Dalgleish have never been questioned. They were merely interviewed, the same as anyone else might be interviewed in the course of an inquiry, who might have information relevant to the matter under investigation.
This statement is made in answer to the request made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) on Friday last, the 14th instant.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
On Friday the leader of
the opposition and my hon. friend the member for Vancouver South made certain inquiries with regard to training camps, and certain comments thereon, and I propose to deal with them and to give the committee such information as I can in this regard. As I indicated to the committee at that time, I felt that it was necessary, although it seemed to me that this was not the place to do it, to deal with some of the matters which have been referred to by the leader of the opposition in connection with some expenditures which have been made at Debert camp and at Fredericton.
There was a vague insinuation by my hon. friend that a man named Mackenzie, of Truro, was favoured in connection with a purchase of materials because of the fact of his political affiliation. I do not know Mr. Mackenzie; I do not know anything about his occupation; and therefore I got some information from the gentleman who dealt with him.
Hon. members will understand that the purchase of timber which was made for Debert camp, amounting to something like 26 million feet, was not made by the Department
of National Defence, but by the Department of Munitions and Supply through the timber controller's office.
At that time the timber controller was Mr. H. R. MacMillan. I inquired from Mr. Loren Brown, who succeeded Mr. MacMillan as timber controller. Mr. Brown communicated with Mr. McCabe, who was referred to by my hon. friend as being the man who actually made the purchase of this lumber; and here is a telegram which Mr. McCabe has sent to Mr. Brown and which Mr. Brown handed to me.
Reference lumber purchase from H. J. Mackenzie, this lumber bought in good faith from Mackenzie who represented himself as a lumber dealer and I was not aware of any different status. The prices were fair and reasonable in fact considerably lower than other competitive market prices. Before leaving Debert the bulk of the stock had been delivered, was up to standards specified and measurement correct, as I gave it personal examination.
I do not know what my hon. friend had in mind in referring to this matter. Down in Nova Scotia, so far as I know, the people generally speaking belong to one of two parties, either the Conservative or the Liberal party. Apparently Mr. Mackenzie happened to be a Liberal. Mr. McCabe says-and Mr. McCabe was given a certificate of character by the leader of the opposition-that he purchased this lumber from Mr. Mackenzie at prices considerably lower than other competitive market prices, that the stock was up to the standard specified, and the measurement was correct. I really do not know what object or what idea my hon. friend had in bringing up this matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The point was this, if the minister will allow me-that Mr. Mackenzie was not a producer, but a middleman.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
suggest that Mr. McCabe did something wrong in not purchasing from a producer; that he has to go to a producer, he cannot purchase from anyone else who buys lumber? I submit that that is a new principle, and in enunciating it he is condemning Mr. McCabe and nobody else. As a matter of fact, Mr. McCabe, so far as I can learn, is an estimable man, and a good lumber purchaser. He purchased as cheaply as he could, at competitive prices, and at prices, he says, lower than were some others.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Does the minister say that Mackenzie was a lumber dealer?

War Appropriation Bill

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I do not know whether Mackenzie was a lumber dealer or not. I have no idea, and I say it does not make any difference, if the lumber was purchased at fair prices and prices even lower than were paid to other people. The prices paid for this lumber were certified as being fair and reasonable by the timber controller or his office at that time; and from what Mr. Brown tells me, and from my hon. friend's own recommendation of Mr. McCabe I think the committee can be satisfied that Mr. McCabe, in making this purchase, was not influenced by any consideration other than obtaining the required lumber at the proper prices. I submit that that ought to be enough. I submit with deference that the time of this committee should not be taken up with it. My hon. friend ought to have known this. He has made inquiries from the timber controller, but he saw fit to bring this matter up in the committee, and take up the time of the house, and bring the hon. member for Colchester into it, and ask him a question which I submit should not have been asked by one hon. member of another on the floor of this chamber, in order to cast some smear of political influence over this transaction.
But I have not finished with that. There was a small quantity purchased from Mackenzie, Mr. Chairman. Do you know how much? There was 26 million feet purchased at Debert, and the total amount sold by Mackenzie consisted of two lots of 100,000 feet each, and another of 80,000 feet, 280,000 in all, or a little over one per cent of the lumber which was purchased at Debert.
Now, my hon. friend says that the lumber companies which he represents-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I did not say anything about the lumber companies which I represent.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend forgets.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If I did, that was an error.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Well, I read it in Hansard this morning. I want to be clear about it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
What
page?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

I will find it in a moment. Page 1560:
I happen to have had something to do with lumbering, and the mills I represented never in their lives got $35 for hemlock.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
If the minister will allow me: I used the past tense,
he used the present tense. There is quite a difference. I do not represent any lumber mills to-day, but for many years I represented many lumber mills in the business world of Canada-quite large ones.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend, as he knows-and it is no disgrace whatever, and no insinuation goes with it-
Mr-. HANSON (York-Sunbury): Then why use the word "represents"? That was an improper thing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Well, then, "represented." I am going to deal with the companies he represented-if that is good enough. The company he represented was, I am sure, the Fraser company. I have no doubt about that. Let us take the Fraser company and the payments made to them as compared with the payments made to Mackenzie. By the way, my hon. friend said something about the Fraser company not having been paid S35 for hemlock, never in their lives having got $35 for hemlock. Anybody would think that they were selling hemlock to the government and not being able to get $35 for it. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that the Fraser company do not even list hemlock and do not sell it at the present time, but he rather gave the impression that they were selling to the government and did not get $35 for it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I did not say anything of the sort. That is the kind of special pleading for which my hon. friend is famous.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I gave my hon. friend the right to speak, but I will not give him permission to interrupt me. My hon. friend referred to the companies he represented, let us say in the past, and I say that my hon. friend is suggesting that in some way or another Mackenzie got some advantage because of the fact that he happened to be of a certain political faith. That was the suggestion. If that was not the suggestion, I do not know what it was.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: All right let it go.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Now, on September 6, Mackenzie sold 100,000 feet of 1 by 4, up 6/16 feet, merchantable hemlock, dressed on one side, at $31. That was delivered by truck on the job at Debert. Fraser Brothers' list price at that time for a quality of lumber which was inferior to that-although it was not
War Appropriation Bill

hemlock-fifth quality spruce, 1 by 6 boards- and that is inferior to merchantable hemlock-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is that so?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
-was $33 delivered
Montreal, $31.50 f.o.b. cars, or, translating it into the Debert figures, according to the timber controller, it would be $33 delivered by truck at Debert, compared with $31 paid to Mackenzie.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Who said the spruce was inferior?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The timber controller,
and anybody else. Would my hon. friend say the contrary?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I certainly say that spruce is superior to hemlock.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
In other words, Mackenzie's merchantable hemlock was better than Fraser's fifth quality and better spruce and sold at $2 less than Fraser's price. That is one instance with respect to the company which my hon. friend represented.
Secondly, Mackenzie sold 100,000 feet of 1 by 5, up 8/16 feet in length, of merchantable spruce, dressed on one side, and in that case he got $32 for it. That also is better lumber, I am informed, than lumber quoted by Fraser's in their list, at a price which would net $33 to the department instead of $32.
So much for that. The next lot was 80,000 feet of spruce, 1 by 5, up 8/16 feet in length, merchantable spruce, dressed on one side, matched, finished 25/32 of an inch off the face, and he got $33 for that. That was delivered by truck on the job; that is sheathing. Fraser, on the other hand, sold to the timber controller fifth quality and better spruce sheathing, $31.70 f.o.b. ears at South Nelson. With freight added, they were paying Fraser Brothers $34.20 for what Mackenzie supplied at $33.
I find no fault with the timber controller for doing that, but I say to my hon. friend that, when he starts in to insinuate there is something wrong with this particular transaction, he had better compare it with those of people he knows something about.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The only thing I think was wrong about it, and the only thing-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
-I had in mind was that it was bought from a man who

was not a producer, not in the lumber business, when it should have been bought direct from the producer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Then my hon. friend's quarrel is with his friend Mr. McCabe and not with the department.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: All right, we will let it go at that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No, we will not let it go at that. In other words, Fraser sheathing may have had a slight advantage in finish because it is finished on both sides and you might allow fifty cents difference for that, although there is really no extra cost in planing both sides. The Fraser sheathing was a lower grade, fifth quality, as against Mackenzie's which was merchantable grade, and it was sold at $1.20 more than Mackenzie's.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But there is a difference in cost for finish on both sides.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have given credit for fifty cents for finish on both sides, and still it is seventy cents above Mackenzie's lumber.
My hon. friend talked about "mills I represented" never getting $35 for hemlock. I have already said the mills he represented were not selling hemlock last fall.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
How do
you know they were not?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Because the timber controller tells me, and the hemlock is not listed by Frasers.
Now about the price paid for hemlock. This is my hon. friend's statement:
Just imagine paying $31 to $35 a thousand for hemlock. Anybody in eastern Canada who knows anything about it knorvs that is a very high price. I have statements on my files upstairs showing that prices of $31 to $35 were paid for planed hemlock. The Minister of National Defence for Air, who comes from a lumbering family, will know what scandalous waste there is in paying prices like that.
Later he said $20 would be a big price.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: So it is, for hemlock boards.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Well, I had my officers go over a thousand acceptances of tender in order to find the price that he says was paid for hemlock. I am surprised that my hon. friend did not bring it down instead of talking about its being up on his table. It is true that S35 was paid for 20,000 feet of hemlock-note that that is less than one-tenth of one per cent of the lumber that was used at Debert. It was for 2 by 6, ten feet long and up, of merchantable hemlock, and $37 was paid for

War Appropriation Bill
forty thousand feet of 2 by 8, 10 feet and up, merchantable hemlock. The timber controller at that time was H. R. MacMillan, and his officials certified that that was a fair and reasonable price. I say that as evidence against my hon. friend's statement about its being a scandalous waste. He did not even give the size; he did not indicate that it was 2 by 6 and 2 by 8, minimum 10-foot lengths.
I wonder that my hon. friend did not in his statement give the firm from which that lumber was bought.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I did not know anything about it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Well, I will tell him. It was bought from Ralph and Arthur Parsons. They are a concern in Windsor, Hants county, Nova Scotia-reputable people, probably as strong Conservatives as there are in Nova Scotia. I knew their father very well. He was in opposition in the provincial house when I happened to be there, and opposed the present premier of Nova Scotia in Hants county. If my hon. friend had told the committee that the S35 was paid, not to some bad Grit, but to a firm who are his own political friends, the story would not have sounded so well. It took me half a day or more of going over files to find out what the situation was. I make no charge whatever against Ralph and Arthur Parsons. They are reputable people, so far as I know and believe. I make no charge against Mr. McCabe for having paid it; but my hon. friend did not do himself justice when he talked about hemlock at 820 a thousand when the timber controller himself has paid $35 and $37 to my hon. friend's own political friends for the same sort of lumber.
My hon. friend talked about ten-inch lumber planed on four sides, and this was his complaint:
Requisitions were made on the Department of Munitions and Supply by the Department of National Defence for lumber of a kind and quality and of specifications which under normal lumber manufacturing conditions in eastern Canada could not readily be supplied in the quantities wanted. The big mills are manufacturing their stocks to-day based largely on the quality and calibre of the round Togs which are delivered to them, and which the sawyer has to utilize to get every foot he can out of the logs. It is used for floor beams and sills, the two finished pieces spiked together, making by that process a 4 by 10. In spiking them together the joints are staggered; you do not have the same thing as a single piece of 4 by 10, but the joints are broken, with the result that you get a stronger piece of timber.
The reason for the planing on four sides, about which my hon. friend complained, is, in the first place, that there is a saving in weight and therefore in freight cost. The planed material packs into a smaller space than rough lumber and is appreciably less in weight. Secondly, the planed stuff is more easily handled and therefore the work can proceed just that much more quickly. Third, it gives uniform dimensions. I think my hon. friend knows quite a bit about lumber, and he knows that rough planks-and these are rough planks-are not sawn to the exact eighth or quarter of an inch. You have to put your planks on edge to make floor beams with a post underneath, and if you have them rough-sawn, and you have to shim up in order to take care of the irregularity which exists because of the sawing. That is all done away with when you have planed, dressed pieces of timber of uniform width. Then, again, the surface of the rough lumber is not true for nailing on the floors, because there is a certain amount of unevenness and waviness since there is not the same care taken in running a piece of lumber through a big saw that there is when you run it through a planer. Fourth, with that rough lumber, the faces do not fit tightly, and therefore strength is lost.
Let me say further, and probably he knows this, too, that I am instructed that the cost of planing on four sides is practically the same as the cost of planing on two. Probably there is a little difference in power, that is all-because you have a planer with four heads, which does the same operation at one time. Our engineers advise that it is economical to have lumber planed on four sides, that it is efficient, and a common practice, and that narrow widths are uneconomical for floor beams or joists.

Well, in all kindness I suggest to my hon. friend that he should not be so gullible when people represent things to him.
Now I should like to say a word to the hon. member for Vancouver South with regard to recruits under the National Resources Mobilization Act. I believe what the hon. gentleman had in mind was the place of recruits under that measure in the scheme of our army problem, where they fit in. First, it seems hardly necessary to repeat what has been said so many times, that the training under the National Resources Mobilization Act is for the purpose of possible needs in regard to home defence. The act itself expressly provides that the service for which men may be called out under the act is service in Canada or the territorial waters thereof.
Now may I recall the situation last summer, which has been referred to by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, who spoke about hurry, haste and things of that kind. The unexpected had happened. The break-through had occurred; and the capitulation of Holland, Belgium and France followed the extension of German operations in Norway. No one knew what might happen. Every effort was bent to take all the measures possible to provide for the most serious contingencies. The possibilities were visualized in that fighting speech by Mr. Churchill early in June. Let me remind the house of the words with which that speech was concluded:
And even if, which I do not for a moment believe, this island or a large part of it were subjugated and starving, then our empire beyond the seas, armed and guarded by the British fleet, will carry on its struggle until in God's good time the new world with all its power and might sets forth to the liberation and rescue of the old.
All that seems to have been forgotten by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). He implies in some way that speed and rapid action could have been avoided. I say that speed was essential. It was considered essential by everybody. The cry was "Get on with it-cut the red tape- never mind the cost." We got on with it, and the story of those hectic, hard-riding days from June to November is one which is, I think, a credit to the officers and men who put forward herculean efforts to get the job done.
In Canada we authorized the recruiting, up to full strength, of the non-permanent active militia, now known as the reserve army, which to-day is over 100,000 strong, apart from those who were trained and posted from the military training centres.

Yes. To be exact, I think it is 177,000. There were 102,000 in the reserve army and around 75,000 posted from the militia training centres.
The time for the dispatch of the second Canadian division was advanced, and the announcement was made that a Canadian corps would be formed overseas. Authority was given for raising the third and fourth Canadian divisions and some additional battalions as well, and for the mobilization of thousands more of ancillary troops of the active army. Another squadron of the Royal Canadian Air Force was authorized for dispatch overseas, and authorization was given for the dispatch of Canadian troops to Newfoundland, Iceland and the Caribbean. Emergency steps were taken to increase the output of pilots and airmen both within and outside the air training plan, and hon. members will remember the pressure that was brought to bear to see if that plan could not be advanced. The veterans home guard was authorized. Every department of our war programme was speeded up, modified and supplemented in the most effective way possible having regard to the interests of Britain and our allies and the part that Canada must play. We announced many other measures which we thought were necessary in view of the menace which had so suddenly arisen. No criticism of these steps was raised, nor could it have been fairly raised by anyone at that time. The action taken was in keeping with that instituted by Mr. Churchill's government which in May created the forces that are known as the local defence forces and proceeded to the registration of almost 1,000,000 more young men preparatory to calling them up for service. The pressure was to do more, not less; and to provide for these contingencies the National Resources Mobilization Act was passed.
Then came the question of how best we could give our citizens some training having regard to the facilities and equipment available. The whole matter was fully discussed

and considered by the staff and by the government. There were two essentials; the preparation of accommodation and the training of instructional staffs, and that required weeks and possibly months to accomplish. The length of the training period had to be arranged so that equipment could be provided, and at the same time it was felt to be highly desirable in the early days to inculcate into the minds of young Canadians their responsibility as citizens. The thirty-day period was adopted as meeting these conditions. There was no thought or suggestion

hon. members will not find it in any statement in Hansard or in any public statement by any member of this government-that thirty days' training would fit a man to take his place as a trained soldier in a fighting unit. Therefore, to take time to argue that a period of thirty days is not enough for that purpose is to set up a straw man to knock him down. There was no mystery and no politics about the thirty-day decision. The decision was made realistically, based on the situation as it existed, and based on the possibilities as they could be judged regarding the course of the war and Canada's means of waging it.
The staffs were carefully selected. These staffs were put through an intensive course of training for the responsibility which they were required to assume. Instruction and the preparation of thirty-nine centres across Canada were commenced, and by October 20 these centres were ready to take classes. Three thirty-day training periods have been held, with the result that more than 75,000 young men in Canada have had the benefit of what is probably the most effective and efficient course of basic training that has ever been furnished to men in this country in thirty days' time. They have learned something of the fundamentals of soldiering, the use of the basic arms, and they have had the benefit of the physical training and the discipline that go with army life. The training they have already had forms a most useful foundation for their complete preparation for service in the defence of Canada should they be called on.
More than that, I believe that the training and the experience they have had will be found an incentive to many of them to volunteer for active sendee should the call come.

Or, to put it the other way, if we did not have the military training centres to-day, we would have had to set about building them for the training of reinforcements against the time when the maximum number might be needed.
As I stated in the house last November, there were two points about the thirty-day training plan which made modification desirable, if that could be done. One was the shortness of the period. The other point was the disturbing effect which the calling-up of these men had on industry; for 30,000 a month for ten months would have meant that
300,000	would have had to make arrangements to leave their civilian occupations for one month in the year. On this latter point I have repeatedly stated that the army has recognized the necessity for the maximum possible production in this country. But with the improvement in production and supply, the equipment situation is no longer a vital factor in preventing the adoption of a longer period.
In order to make allowance for industry, we wanted to consider whether it would be necessary to adopt a system of reserve occupations such as they have in England, or whether some other plan could be evolved which would cause a minimum of dislocation, without the complicated system of reserve
occupations and the enormous amount of machinery necessary to administer it. We studied the situation overseas. We found, on examining the system of reserved occupations there, that it would be highly desirable, if it could be done and still supply our needs, to work out some plan which would avoid our having to set up machinery and prescribe arbitrarily classifications and subclassifications to be excepted. On our return the present plan was worked out. It provides for four months' training-two months' basic training and two months' advanced training. This means that future additions to the reserve will be completely trained in all weapons with which, as individuals, they may be called upon to fight. It avoids the system of reserved occupations by the simple expedient of confining the calls to a very much limited group unless circumstances change materially or the numbers in this group should prove unexpectedly small. It also embodies this desirable feature, that young men at the time of their coming of age are reminded to recognize and prepare themselves for their responsibilities for the defence of Canada.
The question is asked: How does this fit in with our general army programme? What we are doing is to combine certain training facilities and establishments for training in the active army with facilities and establishments we shall be using for the training of those called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act and to help to create a trained reserve for the defence of Canada.
By and large, the military training centres which have been used for training the three classes already held under the National Resources Mobilization Act will be used for the basic training of both the active and the National Resources Mobilization Act personnel.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend is assuming something I do not admit. They are permitted to carry on with these other units. He says that they are names on a piece of paper. They are members of a reserve unit, and these were the instructions given. I think I am correct when I say that we expressly provided that these men, if attending training classes, were allowed pay similarly to other reserve personnel for the time they trained. It may be that there is not sufficient encouragement, but certainly the instructions were that they were to be treated exactly as members of that particular unit. My hon. friend cites a case the opposite of that mentioned by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling). He suggests an instance where the men who are trained are close to a reserve unit and, if possible, that case ought to be met. He is absolutely right in assuming that these men will provide some strength for the reserve unit. They have had intensive training, more intensive than the reserve unit can give. As a humble officer of a militia unit for a time, I remember how sketchy any training was that I was able to give the poor devils under me. But these men know something about training; they have had it intensively. The same applies where they are needed in connection with defence if there is a call. These men, particularly those trained for four months, would be a tremendous help, and an additional strength to a unit which might be called out for the defence of Canada. going to the militia to train two nights a week; I know more than they do." That is due to the way the government has handled it. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

I am ready to be convicted if I have done something wrong or neglected to do something I should have done; the government the hon. member refers to, is your humble servant in connection with this matter, and I should be glad to know wherein we have handled the matter badly and how we can improve it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: May I interrupt there? My hon. friend knows that up until a short time ago nobody could be attested in the reserve units. Recruiting stopped on August 15 and there was no recruiting for the reserve units. My hon. friend knows further that units have now been authorized to fill up to full strength, and as they supply reinforcements or as their ranks are reduced in any way, they have been authorized to recruit. These men can enlist for that purpose the

same as anyone else. But I am still waiting for my hon. friend to tell me what I can do to better the situation. Does he think we should make an order requiring these men to go to drill at headquarters after they have done their training?

Certainly. Why spend all this money giving these men all this training and then simply send them back to civilian life so that they are gone unless Canada is attacked? Why not have the regulations such that they go into a reserve unit?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They are not attested in a reserve unit?
You do not have to attest them; they are on the roll.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is not the difference that they fall into two classes? Prior to the reserve army being what it is now, to belong to the non-permanent active militia unit a man was attested, and when he received notice that drill was on a certain night he had to be there or he was subject to a fine. We have added to that now between 72,000 and 80,000 men who are not in that position but are in the position that they have done their training and are told that as a result of the regulations of the department they are now part of the reserve. The only way their services can be utilized is to use the pressure which you can use under the National Resources Mobilization Act and call them out for service in camp.

Right, or by reason of
their being posted to the unit.

In connection with this
matter of enlisting for reserve units now, are the men who enlist required to undertake to go on active service?

There is no regulation
requiring it.
They are in some districts, are they not?

Not that I know of. There are no instructions to that effect. The instructions are that as far sis possible officers will endeavour to see that men are of a medical category which would make them acceptable.
I do not mean that.
There are no instructions other than that.
I had in mind seeing in the press in my own city a statement that no recruits would be taken for the 2nd battalion unless they undertook to go on active service.

That is the 2nd battalion that is responsible for that. It is not under instructions.

War Appropriation Bill
Have they authority to do that? It does not seem to be the law.
I suppose the commanding officer might say, "I will not take anyone who will not agree to go overseas."

A little
pressure. With respect to the thirty-day training, is not this the position in a nutshell, that they are part of the non-^permanent army de jure, but de facto they are not? If they are not joined up the instmction will in time be lost to the country. That is the principle I was arguing for. Will they not go back? I am told they will. The minister knows more about it than I do, but there seems to be a gap with respect to these trainees and their usefulness to the country after a large sum has been spent on their training. That is what I was trying to argue on Friday, only for the extension to overseas service. If the situation gets bad enough I think that ought to be done. The question of policy will have to be worked out in the course of time, subject to the trend of events. At the moment it is not necessary, but we ought to take a long view, and I suggest that one of the first questions the minister should consider is: how can these young men be made more effective for (a) non-active service and (b) active service, so that the country will not lose the benefit of the expenditure incurred for their instruction and training. This is offered in good faith, I suggest that the government give attention to the whole position in that regard.

I know the suggestion is offered in good faith. I have told the committee what has been done in that respect. I certainly shall give the suggestions of the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Vancouver South and other hon. members regarding a closer tie-up between these men who have been trained and the reserve units the very best study I can. The first thing to do, however, is to get this plan started; hon. members perhaps do not realize the administrative and instructional difficulties there are in setting up these schools and installing new instructors.

I should like to make a statement and ask a question so that I may get the facts definitely. As I understand it, it is now proposed that when men leave training they shall be attached actively to these various units, such as the Seaforth Highlanders?
The word is "posted".

They are attached already in the sense that when they leave the training

camp they are part of the reserve army. Let us take, say, the Seaforth Highlanders. There are openings for a relatively small number of men, say 50 or 60. You have leaving camp a much larger number, say 1,000. If you are going to say to these 1,000 men, not merely "You are attached to the reserve army", but "You are attached to the Seaforth Highlanders", then you have the Seaforth Highlanders badly swollen, and you will have difficulty in getting 1,000 of them into a place where fifty ought to be. It seems to me that is so.
Then, if you do not put the whole 1,000 of them actually into the reserve army, you are up against the proposition of deciding which fifty out of the 1,000 you will choose. This is a point to which I believe those who are advocating placing these persons in the reserve must address themselves, and unless they can offer something constructive in that respect, then nothing constructive has been offered at all. I may be wrong in that, but from the picture I have drawn from what has been said this afternoon, as well as what people have said to me from time to time, that is the problem as I see it.
You cannot put a whole 1,000 men into a particular regiment, and therefore you are up against the problem as to which ones you shall choose to take the regular training.
It could be done by selectors.
If that is what is being proposed, namely, something in the nature of selective draft for continued home service, all right; let us know about it. But it has not been worked out so far.

In reply to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, I would point out that there have been only 25.000 in each thirty-day period in the whole of Canada; and, as I understand it, all of these men have been posted to infantry units. There are other units-artillery, engineers, medical corps, and so on; and I say that they should be posted to and train with some particular unit-not necessarily an infantry unit, but some reserve unit. If necessary, a third battalion could be made of the infantry regiments.
Are they under strength?

The point is that those men should be posted and actively training with some militia unit. Under the new plan we are going to have only 5,000 a month for the whole of Canada. There can be no question that there is plenty of room to absorb that number across Canada. I do not see how there can be any excuse now for simply turning back those 5,000 into civil life, and not putting them into a reserve unit.

War Appropriation Bill
And letting them make the choice of unit.

Before the minister continues, I believe it is felt in many circles that a great deal of money is being spent on the training of these men, and that unless that training is followed up, the value of it will be almost nil. I believe we are talking at cross purposes when we say that these men are attached.
Posted.
They are not posted; they are attached.
"Posted" is the word.

Let me place before the committee a specific instance: The unit in which I am interested is a unit which is well over strength. There are something over 1,400 men in that reserve unit. There are attached or posted to it over 1,500 of these men who have taken thirty days' training. What does it mean? It simply means that some files are carried into the adjutant's office, and that they are put into a corner.
I would assume that the 1,500 men live nowhere near the unit.
They live in the area from which the unit is recruited.

I believe that is taken care of, from the point of view of administration, and from the point of view from which hon. members have approached it, by the fact that they are posted (a) to the reserve unit in the locality, or (b) to corps reserve.

As the minister states, this unit covers a considerable area. There are four rifle companies, and a headquarters company. In each of the larger towns in that area there is a company commander, and sometimes a company sergeant-major, who are responsible in the particular area from which the company is recruited for part-time training. Then they are brought together to battalion headquarters, annually, for annual training.
These men-and possibly I should use the term "trainees"-have no feeling of unity with the company or area in which they live. They are not called in for training, because the company is already over-strength. They are not called for training in the battalion. There is a cleavage there, and considerable feeling has arisen in that connection. These men do not belong to any company; they are not attached to any particular company, and are not in any platoon. They do not go to training with that unit. As a matter of fact,
they are not part of the unit at all, except that their names are in the same files in the adjutant's office.
The minister has asked for some suggestion. I do not think they can be merged into a unit which is already over-strength. I do not see why another battalion could not be formed, and these men become a reserve battalion. Where one company is now training, two companies could be trained. These men who have taken thirty days' training would have a company or a platoon to which they could go, and with which they would train, having exactly the same routine they would go through if they were members of the reserve army. Otherwise they do not feel any attachment to the unit with which they are posted. Unless something of the sort is done within the year, I believe the money the Canadian people have spent on this project will have pretty well filtered away. That will happen, unless there is some way of keeping these men attached to some unit, with contacts through non-commissioned officers, officers and in this way develop an esprit de corps.

I do not believe I need take further time in committee by adding to what I have already said. I shall certainly take note of the observations of hon. members, and I want them to take note of what has already been done. I believe the hon. member who spoke last had the gist of the matter when he said that this was not an immediate thing. But I can see the point they are making, and therefore I will give it the best study I can.

What will be done in the event of a trainee changing his place of residence? Is there any provision whereby he would be followed up? Is there a provision that he shall notify the authorities in the event of a change of residence, or may he easily be lost?
I do not think there is any provision, but he is in the unit to which he has been attached.

What provision is made for enlisting these trainees in the various fighting forces? What encouragement is given to them to enlist? I have been told that while the navy and the air force are fairly active in the camps, trying to have these young men enlist in their respective forces, the army is not doing so. I understand the army makes little or no attempt to persuade the young men to enlist in the active service force. Is that so? What provisions have been made whereby it is made easy for one of these young men to enlist in the active army?

I cannot say that any provisions are made, or that any pressure is brought upon them to enlist. As my hon.
War Appropriation Bill

friend and the committee know, and as I said the other day to the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough, so far we have had sufficient enlistments to take care of our reenforcement requirements. The trouble is- if it is a trouble-that we have in Canada a great many men who are impatient for overseas service. Casualties have not occurred. Our reenforcements are more than up to requirements, and therefore there is not the call for recruits.
I may say that the navy, the army and the air force have a committee working at the present time with a view to what may be a joint recruiting call, having regard to the needs of the three services which we visualize this summer may be required by reason of formations going overseas. But, answering my hon. friend's question, there has not been any intensive recruiting campaign. As I said to the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough, our difficulty is that we cannot put on these evangelistic campaigns in this war, as we did in the last one, because the need is not there as yet at least. People are complaining that we are interfering with industry, with farming and with everything else; they ask what we are going to do with the men when we do enlist them. No one realizes better than I do the fact that this has a dampening effect upon recruiting. I do not say we have not ideas in the department with regard to the matter; we have, but I would welcome any suggestions which might be made by any one in this connection.
Answering my hon. friend, there is no special effort made to get these men to enlist. What was done, as my hon. friend knows and as the house has been told, was this. They were asked in the camp whether, if an opportunity to enlist should come, they would be willing to do so. The figures I received were what I gave my hon. friend the leader of the opposition this afternoon; namely, that taking the navy, the army and the air force, about twenty-five per cent expressed their willingness to enlist if required.
Of that number how many have actually enlisted?

I cannot tell my hon.
friend.

Or have that twenty-five
per cent been given an actual opportunity to enlist?

I am telling my hon. friend the opportunity is there all the time. The way enlistments are called for is this. If a call comes from overseas for reinforcements, or if the adjutant general's office feels

that in some particular service there is necessity for reinforcements, a quota is immediately made up of the reinforcements required, and that quota is apportioned to the different districts all over Canada; each district is asked for so many men. My hon. friend knows this procedure, I am sure. They have their district depots where men have enlisted, from which they have gone to the training centres; and these recruits are called for from these different training centres. Then, if there is need for more men for enlistment in place of these reinforcements, the militia units in that particular area are told that so many men are required, and they are given an opportunity to have their personnel enlist for that purpose. That is the way in which recruiting is done generally, through the militia unit. There are not usually general calls. Of course there are men from time to time who come directly to the recruiting office from the street. They enlist, and they are received, of course.

If the
minister will allow me, is that quite so? In the filling up of the quotas to which he has just referred, from the military district, is there an opportunity every day for men to enlist in the active service army? I have been told, and I should like to be corrected if I am wrong-it seems that I am very wrong most of the time, according to the minister this afternoon-

We are talking about
something else now.
I want to know if there is an opportunity to enlist six days in the week, whether quotas are filled up or not.
No, I would not say so.
The opportunity for enlistment is very limited indeed, is it not?
That is correct.
Then let us have that perfectly clear. Until there is the need of men for the active army, whether it be for service in Canada or overseas, that opportunity will continue to be very much restricted?
That is so.

Well, I
think that is a fair statement.

In the case of these men who are anxious to join the army would it not be wise to let them enlist at once, even though it meant expanding the force to a

15S9
certain degree? Now that only 5,000 are being trained each month there will not be such large numbers of these men available, and surely when a man in the camp wants to enlist in the forces it should be possible for him to do so, even though it means making the forces a little larger than had been planned. It is far better for us to have too many men trained and under arms in this country, in this terrible crisis, than to have too few.

I can only say to my
hon. friend that there I am guided by the staff. I am assured that we have ample men in Canada under this plan for any possible forseeable need for home defence. As far as the situation overseas is concerned we have ample men at the present time-I just say at the present time-for reinforcements for the troops who are overseas. The leader of the opposition has put his finger on the main point, namely, that until there are casualties or some need arises because of these formations going overseas, there is not the opportunity for any widespread enlistment. My hon. friend asks if we could not give that opportunity to a few men. What I think he has in mind is to utilize the four months' training of these men. I will give consideration to that point, as to whether possibly some special consideration could not be given in these circumstances because, as my hon. friend says, there we have trained men.

In addition to the reason that has been given by the minister, is there not the further reason that the equipment and accommodation are not available and would require considerable extension. Is that not about right?
I would think so.

I think
that is a fair statement.

In this country there are
representatives of a number of free governments, the Polish, the Norwegian, the Dutch and more recently the Belgian. They have troops in training centres in various parts of the country. What assistance, if any, is being given by the government of Canada or the Department of National Defence to these groups? What financial assistance is being given?
To give my question more force, I should like to point out to the minister that recently the Polish group appear to have had some difficulties. They have been moving from one city to another in an endeavour to find quarters for the training of their men. I think it is desirable that the minister make a statement in regard to this matter, because
I know it has caused some inconvenience and, with no desire to magnify it at all, I believe there has been some friction. Are we rendering any assistance to these movements? If so, what is that assistance, and should it not go further and actually help them to get established in various communities? This difficulty now exists, and I should be very grateful if the minister would say a word about it.

All I can say to my hon. friend is that this is a matter for the Department of External Affairs rather than for the Department of National Defence. The assistance which is given in this connection and the arrangements which have been made have been the subject of correspondence between the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the representatives of the various governments. I am not in a position to give my hon. friend any information beyond that at the moment.
When I was home last I was interviewed by a number of soldiers who had recently returned from England, for reasons into which I made no inquiry. They find it impossible to obtain positions.
These are discharged men?

Yes; and after having been in the army for a year, more or less, they are almost unfit for employment right away. Could not the Department of National Defence connect up or work with the Department of Munitions and Supply or the Department of Labour in an endeavour to bring about the employment of these returned soldiers in some of the large factories or on some of the building programmes under the control of the department? It seems to me too bad that these men should be brought back from England and have nothing to do here. The government is financing or assisting to finance many large projects, and I do not see why the various departments could not cooperate in order to place many of these men. It is bad enough to be out of work at any time, but it is worse for a returned soldier coming home to be out of a job. Something should be done in this connection. If nothing is done it may result in the men saying things they should not say, after having been in the army and then out of it. It would relieve their anxiety if the government would see that they are placed in some of the government projects.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

To answer for my colleague, the Minister of Pensions and National Health, there was put through by order in council

some time ago what is known as a rehabilitation plan which I think awards one month's pay to those who have been discharged from the army. If the man is unfit owing to his war service he obtains a pension. If he is not, the Department of Pensions and National Health is reorganizing the rehabilitation branch, and the Minister of Pensions and National Health has recently created the position of associate deputy minister to look after rehabilitation. The veterans assistance committees in days gone by did do a valuable work. They are in touch with industry throughout the country, and they would appear to be the appropriate coordinating body as between the discharged soldier and the new industries which are being set up. I do know that the Minister of Pensions and National Health has large plans along these lines, but to what extent these plans have been completed I am not in a position to say.

The minister must have read that at the recent labour conference resolutions were passed recommending that the government keep on the payroll, until they obtain employment, soldiers who have now returned. Has the minister anything to offer in that connection?

I want to come to the support of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). I do not think he usually requires support, but on this occasion I think he

War Appropriation Bill

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: My hon. friend will have to appeal to the generosity of the Minister of Pensions.

The Minister of National Defence has stated that many of the trainees have volunteered to join the service. I have been concerned with the set-up of our reserve army, if something should happen overseas, which we all trust will not happen, necessitating large numbers of reinforcements. I think we should be training a reserve army immediately for reinforcements. Has the minister considered with his staff, training a reserve army composed of those within the required categories who could be transferred for training to active service? In the whole set-up of the reserve army it seems to me that we are not getting value in man-power or for the money spent should a sudden demand for reinforcements arise.

My hon. friend is mixing up two things. The reserve army is not for reinforcements for overseas except to the extent that the men volunteer. The staff have advised that so far as Canada's defence is concerned, our reserves are adequate. We know what our resources are overseas and what we plan for, and I have given the committee a list of the formations we are going to have. We feel satisfied that we can provide ample reinforcements for them. I do not know just what my hon. friend has in his mind when he says he is not satisfied with the set-up. We have 175,000 trainees in all in the reserve army, some with thirty days' training and some with longer periods. In addition, we have a great number of men, over 100,000, in the active service force in Canada. The defence of Canada must visualize certain scales of attack. These scales have been weighed and appraised. It is only in certain contingencies that these attacks can occur, and we all realize what will be the situation if they do occur; that is, what additional forces will be available for that purpose. In the light of all that the staff have advised me that we are making ample provision.
Just in that connection, may I be allowed to complete my statement. All these men- that is, these 175,000 men-have completed thirty days' training, and many have, to their credit, years of service in the previous militia. They represent a potential force rather than an actual one at this time because the battle of Britain is being successfully waged, and so long as that continues no heavy attack on Canada will be practical. All these are in addition to the active army formations in Canada.
I can say to the committee that, a careful appraisal having been made of the prospects
and requirements in any emergency which can be reasonably foreseen, it is considered that the plan we have evolved will meet the requirements of home defence. That is not my opinion only but the opinion of the staff who have given most careful consideration to the matter, and who are responsible for advising myself and the government in that connection.
Something has been said regarding the release, to the existing reserve units, of these men who are being trained. What we plan is that where they are in localities which have reserve units, they shall be posted to those units; if they are in localities where there are no reserve units, they will be posted, after the completion of their training, to a corps reserve of the arm in which they have been trained. I have heard what hon. members have suggested in that regard and I assure them- and this is no mere formal assurance-that their suggestions will have the very best study we can give them.
If the unit is needed for home defence, they will form a useful nucleus of trained men to give added strength to that unit; and, on the other hand, as I have said regarding the men who have had thirty days' training, I believe that many of them will, by reason of their experience in army life, be ready to enlist in case a widespread call goes out for recruits for overseas service.
May I emphasize that with the large numbers of partly trained reserve personnel available the sensible course is now to see to it that so far as facilities permit, future additions to that force will be completely trained in the weapons with which, as individuals, they might later be called upon to fight.
Barring changes which no one can foresee, we envisage some 60,000 young men of the twenty-one year old class being called up for four months' compulsory training in the year.
Training this 60,000 for the reserve would allow, in our revised system of basic and advanced training centres, capacity for a further 60,000 per annum of active service personnel of other age groups. Remember that this number is the equivalent of two or two and a half divisions, and is in addition to the men we have partly trained, men of the reserve, and whatever active units there may be in Canada.
In other words, we would expect to train in an adequate and approved manner no less than 120,000 young men in Canada during the next year. Some of these, at the end of two months' basic training, on volunteering will be transferred to the Royal Canadian Navy or Royal Canadian Air Force, and the remainder to the active or reserve army as the case may be.
War Appropriation Bill

Let me make this clear-perhaps it needs to be emphasized a bit. The four months' training plan is not merely a National Resources Mobilization Act plan; it is not merely an active service force plan; it is a Canadian army plan. The plan will, we believe, by training men who have enlisted for overseas service, provide training for the maximum reinforcements needed for overseas. At the same time, through its training of men who are called up for training under the National Resources Mobilization Act, it will provide us with the means to assist in creating a trained reserve force which, in addition to such active units as may be allotted to that task, will suffice to meet the possible demands of home defence.
I believe that the latter part of that statement does meet what the hon. member for Souris -has referred to. It is true that the reserve army is only partly trained, but it is a large army for Canadian defence. There is no doubt about that. What this plan does is to endeavour to put alongside of it-and I am as anxious as anybody to see that it not only puts alongside of but integrates with it- the men who have four months' training, in order that it may be given stiffening and made as effective as possible.
There is not, I suppose, a standing order that these men who are in the reserve army will be in A category?
No.
A great many of these men would be in a lower category and therefore would not be able to transfer.

I should be glad to hear from the committee-although it is a peculiar position for a minister to take-whether the categories of the reserve army should be A and B instead of including C. As the committee knows, it goes down to "C-l." That is a difference between the active and the reserve. The active does take A and B and does not take C.

Has the minister any
information as to how the reserve army is made up in so far as the medical categories are concerned?
The proportion?
Yes.
No; I am sorry I have not. I can get it very easily.
Perhaps it would be of interest to the committee.
It is germane to the question I have just mentioned.

The hon. member for Souris has just asked a question which I intended to ask. There are, however, some further questions I should like to put with regard to the present reserve army units. Will the result of the attachment of these trained men to the established unit change the present training programme in any way? Will it, for instance, change the length of time in camp? Will it change the personnel of the present units? Will the new men have to take the full training of the unit they join? As a matter of fact, I am thinking particularly of the Brockville rifles. By the time the first batch of these men are turned out, it will be just about time for the Brockville rifles to go to camp. These men, I take it, will be attached to the local regiment. They will just have finished four months in camp, and naturally will be far ahead of any training that the local unit will have, and any work they do at camp will appear very elementary to them. Will a special company be set up for them? It would seem to be a waste of effort that they should go through all the elementary training which the normal reserve unit would have to go through.
As I understand it, those who are in my hon. friend's vicinity who are attached to the Brockville Rifles and have finished the four months' training will not go to camp with the Brockville Rifles.
Has the minister given any consideration to the question of the selective draft, that is, covering a wide age group and choosing by lot, rather than taking all the twenty-one year old men?

Yes. That is what I
endeavoured to cover in the first part of the statement I made to the committee a little while ago. "With a selective draft, you immediately get into difficulties with industry. We must face that fact. If we are going to have a selective draft and extend these age groups any distance, I for one believe-I do not know whether all my colleagues agree with me, but perhaps the committee may- that we must have reserved occupations for two purposes: to exempt men of the reserved occupations from being called up for training, and to refuse to accept men who volunteer; that is to say, we would say to men who want to go into the army, "No, you cannot go in because the particular occupation you are in is one so essential to industry that you can better serve your country there."

Is that not what the principle of the selective draft implies? I may be all wrong in my understanding of what the selective principle is,

War Appropriation Bill
but my idea of it was that you could say, "You shall not be selected because you are more valuable to the state in some other capacity." Has that been turned down definitely?

We studied that in England. It involves reserved occupations, and it involves all the machinery of boards and things of that kind, and constant changes of regulations, which we think we have avoided under this system, which simply takes a very much limited age group, and cannot disturb industry seriously, but empowers the board to postpone a certain class, in order that they may have the benefit of pursuing their seasonal occupation, or matter of that kind. It avoids all complications. There was a book prepared a year and a half ago containing lists of reserved occupations; it must have extended to 150 typewritten pages.
That is, in England.

That is what they are worrying over in England at the present time. We may have to come to it. If you take more than these twenty-one year olds you reach the stage where you disturb industry. You may have to do it, but I feel that we do not have to come to it yet, and therefore we propose this simple course of taking the twenty-one year old class, providing for postponement in cases of occupations where postponement is required, but not providing for exemptions. According to the staff, it fully supplies our needs of home defence at the present time.
The young men are not a factor in industry.
Not to the same extent.

I think
we ought to welcome that statement of the minister, whether or not we agree with it.
Some of them are a factor.

My hon. friend is right, some of them are. As a matter of fact, the national labour supply board were talking to me to-day with regard to a few men.
