I know that the mining industry say that they are training some young men; they have some twenty-one year old men in their service. Industry is cooperating in connection with this iplan. We have consulted the national labour supply board; they have been in on all the conferences, and they know what is being planned.
I know of one instance in which an industry was asked, with regard to the thirty-day training, how many men would be affected who were essential to that industry. The manager
sent back word, "175." The general manager did not believe that. He went down and investigated and he found that there were just three men who could not be spared. The same is true of a number of other industries. It is found that there are not many men who cannot be spared for the limited time required. There are some industries which are training young men who fall into the twenty-one year old class, and provision will have to be made in that direction.

Is the position not the same with young men who are being trained in the technical schools under the Minister of Labour? Take young men in their teens, who are receiving training courses for industry. Shortly they will be twenty-one. Are they to go into training camps or will they remain in industry?
The hon. member does not want me to look a year ahead?
That is the trouble. We are looking a couple of days ahead instead of a year.

That is not a fair statement. I ask my hon. friend if anyone in this war can look ahead a year and make plans further than we have made our plans. We have quite sufficient if we make the best plans we can for the formations we are providing for this year and endeavour to meet them with the man-power we have, and I do not think it is quite fair to suggest that these are two-day plans. They are no such thing. I will endeavour to give attention to what my hon. friend suggests, but it is not essential at this moment-
Perhaps not two days, but we are not looking far enough ahead.
Can the minister give a statement of those receiving the thirty-day training, by provinces, and then volunteering for active service?
Another question was asked with reference to information by provinces. I cannot give it by provinces; I can give it only by military districts.
By military districts.

Would it be possible to speed up the report on the men who go for medical examination? Industry hesitates to take the twenty-one year old class unless they have already had training. Industry hesitates to take in a great many of these boys because, in the course of a month or two, just as they are beginning to work at a job, they will be called for training. A great number of them are rejected after medical examination, but
War Appropriation Bill

it is so long between the time they take the medical examination and the time they get their report that it would expedite matters a great deal, so far as industry is concerned, if the report could be received sooner.
That ought to be done.
It would help considerably.
The minister made some reference to the national labour supply board.
Council.

Is there any voice of agriculture with respect to that council, or are they going on their own, as it were, so far as selections are concerned? I am interested in it because we all realize that the shortage of labour on farms is now becoming so acute that something has to be done in that regard, and I should like to see agriculture with some representation so far as the labour supply council is concerned.

As regards the national labour supply council, the Minister of Labour can answer. The Department of National Defence is represented on the labour coordination board, which is the important board after all; I say this with all due respect to the national labour supply council, who are an advisory body. It is not a board which originates and carries out decisions. On the labour board the Minister of National War Services, who is also Minister of Agriculture, has direct representation.
What representation is there so far as industry is concerned?

I do not wish to amplify anything that the Minister of National Defence has said, but in the national labour supply council the representation is directly from manufacturing industry and from labour. As the minister has said, in connection with the interdepartmental committee on labour supply, on which agriculture is represented ad hoc, consideration is being given at the present time to the matter of increased labour supply in that industry.

Can the minister explain just what coordination there is between these two boards? I was talking the other day to a manufacturer who is doing an important job in the war. I asked him whether he was carrying on his ordinary peace-time pursuits and he said, "yes". He had built an addition for what they are doing in connection with the war. As I say, it is an important job, his being the only firm which at the time was in a position to do it. He told me he had taken in thirty farmers' sons from our territory, and in the course of a year he has

made real mechanics of them. He says they are wonderful fellows, coming into industry fresh and strong and with a desire to learn. But there are thirty farmers' sons who have gone into that industry off the farms where they ought to be. It is a serious matter.
In December we had more applications for employment in our plant than we had during the depression, or at least as many. I could not understand it. We kept a record of these men and I wondered why that should be. Then for several days I checked up on the men who came and applied for work. I talked to them personally. Every one was a son of a farmer, a boy who prior to that time had been employed on his father's farm. Now he was asking for work. There are hundreds of boys in Waterloo county who have come off the farms and gone into industry in that county, and it is a serious thing for the farmer. I realize the difficulty of saying to a boy that he must stay on the farm and do that work even though there is not much compensation in it, instead of going into industry and getting higher wages than those paid on the farm. Something should be done. I was wondering whether under our national war services some action could be taken to distribute labour in such a way as not to interfere with production on the farm, because we are going to do it in our county. I know that for a fact.

The difficulty raised by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) is a real one. When you talk about distributing labour, your greatest obstacle is that when you begin to distribute labour among the farmers you strike the low-wage level as against the high-wage level of industry, and perhaps at no time in our history has this matter been as acutely drawn to the attention of the public and of industry as it is to-day. I see advertisements in the papers stating that young men can leave high school and get, I believe, about fifteen dollars a month and board. That is not so very attractive when you put up against it some of the wages paid in industry. It is not a matter of being a demagogue in relation to the farmers of the country; the question is one of acute lack of parity between farm income and the income of many other industries. This disparity has become so apparent that in it lies the fundamental difficulty in distributing labour at the moment. You cannot fairly say to a farmer's son, "You stay where you are and work for next to nothing during the war, while men in other war industries are being paid a high rate of wages".
In that lies the whole kernel of the labour situation. The sooner this government acting

War Appropriation Bill
in conjunction with organized agriculture, comes to the point where something is done to put agriculture on more of a parity with other war industries-because it is a war industry-the sooner we shall be able to distribute labour in the national interest and for the national benefit. While the present lack of parity exists, I can readily understand the position in which the Minister of Labour finds himself in attempting to say to one man, "You stay in a low-wage category" and to another, "You go into a high-wage category." I am not in favour of low wages for the working man; in many instances he is not getting enough; but the solution is not to bring him down but to bring the farmer up, and until we come to that realization we are going to have the troubles this committee is trying to deal with now.

I have listened with great interest to the minister's description of the difficulties of this occupational selection. We ought, however, to take a longer view of this matter. The minister tells us we shall not need the same amount of judicial machinery to do it the way we are going to do it. I hope the war is going to end soon, but that is not the present consensus. The course of the war is going to change; we are going to require more and more goods, more and more war material all the time; we are going to need aeroplanes, guns and munitions. This idea of calling up the twenty-one year old men now is all very well; but some time we shall have to set up this machinery in order to make a proper selection, and appeal board* and that sort of thing, so why not start as soon as we can?
The minister says the twenty-one year old men are the ones who will be least affected. But things change so rapidly these days, by the end of this year we shall probably need all these young men who have been trained not only in the technical schools but many of them in the aeroplane factories as well. Industry is expanding; they will all be needed. Now is the time to start on the selection, rather than doing it this way now and some other way later. We should have some machinery set up now and take the long view.
Did the minister finish his statement?
Yes.
I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence for Air about the construction to be placed on the term, "home war", as used on page 1494 of Hansard.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: With reference to air?
I assume it is with reference to air; I had not heard the term used with 'reference to any other branch.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Usually we divide our estimates into three parts: overseas, home war establishment, and the joint air training plan. The home war establishment is the establishment for the defence of Canada; it operates a certain number of defence stations which are not employed in the training plan. The training plan set-up is kept separate from the home war establishment and overseas.

I want to come back for a moment to the question asked by the hon. member for Davenport. It is an important question, and personally I was not satisfied with the answer. I notice in the break-down of the figures under Pensions and National Health there is an appropriation of S20.000 listed for a committee on demobilization, which indicates that the government are considering the matter of demobilization. To my mind, one of the things that can hurt our war effort most at the present time is to have men who went overseas, did what they could and came back broken in health, some of them wounded, now on the street with just a month's pay and no understanding as to what is going to happen after that. Many of them have dependents.
I notice the British government have enacted legislation providing that a man remains in uniform and is taken care of by the government until he is placed at some gainful occupation. I suppose this committee has been functioning; there is an appropriation for it here and men are being demobilized, but from the answer given by the Minister of National Defence for Air apparently there is not in the department any regulation for or concrete understanding for taking care of these men. I should like to have some more definite answer than was given by the minister.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Rehabilitation is not the business of the Department of National Defence. We cannot do it. The energies of the Department of National Defence are devoted to getting the best type of men and training them to fight. When, however, a man is discharged from the army as no longer fit he should automatically go to another department. I can assure my hon. friend that the business of rehabilitation is big enough to require the work of a department that is not engaged in looking after the fighting services. The department of Pensions and National Health has had the experience of the last twenty years, since the
War Appropriation Bill

last war, in dealing with those questions. That department is setting up the necessary machinery to look after demobilization.
I expect that the committee on demobilization referred to by my hon. friend is a committee being organized by the Minister of Pensions and National Health, with representatives of labour and of industry, and I think some economists, in order to make a thorough study of what should be done with these men when they come back.
While this study is going on in order to formulate a broad general policy, if men are found unfit owing to war service they are pensioned. If they are not unfit owing to war service; if for some reason they are not entitled to pension, then these veterans assistance committees set up in various centres across Canada are going to endeavour to find them positions in industry.
My hon. friend says that the British government keeps such men in uniform until they obtain positions. I am not aware of such legislation as that anywhere; I do not think it would be feasible in this country to keep in the army twenty or thirty or fifty thousand men who are unfit; it would be a burden which the army should not be called upon to bear. These men should go to another department, the rehabilitation department, and I believe steps are being taken to have them do so.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When the committee rose at six o'clock, the Minister of National Defence for Air was replying to a question which had been asked by the hon. member for Davenport with reference to a request made a few days ago by an organization that, with regard to men who had been discharged, the government keep them on the payroll until such time as they are placed in civilian life. The minister's mind is probably too departmentalized in the matter. I do not believe anyone was suggesting that these men should be kept on in the actual army.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That was the suggestion, and it was that suggestion to which I took exception.
It was not suggested by me.

I do not think anyone was suggesting that. The trades and labour congress made the suggestion to the

government, and I do not believe that, in the memorandum submitted, they made the suggestion the minister has indicated. Their suggestion was that those men be kept on the payroll. Whose payroll it is does not matter. It would be on the government payroll. No one was suggesting that these men could be kept on the army's strength, but it was suggested that they should be kept on the government payroll. In other words, the suggestion was that the government should recognize its responsibility to these men, just as these men in turn have recognized their responsibility to the country.
The suggestion that the veterans assistance committees can take care of these men is not practical. These committees have done some excellent work, and I know a number of men they have assisted to reestablishment in civilian life. But as the war goes on, the number of men being discharged is bound to increase, and the committees giving part time to such a task could not possibly meet the situation.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There is a whole department for that work. The Department of Pensions and National Health deals with the matter; that is their job, and it has been their job for twenty years.

It may be their job, but the point I make to the minister is that the job is not being done. There is scarcely a member in the House of Commons who does not know of at least a few cases respecting men who have been discharged. They come in two categories, the first category being those who have pensions coming to them. The minister knows that such pensions do not come by return of mail. The men have to make application, boards have to be set up, and a considerable length of time is required. There is an interim period. What are they to do during that period?
There is the second class of men who are not eligible for pension, and who have to make some adjustments. One month's pay does not begin to tide these men over the period of readjustment. I suggest that some time before this appropriation bill passes we ought to have a statement from the Minister of Pensions and National Health as to exactly what the government's programme is in connection with men returning to Canada for discharge. What is to happen to them during the time their applications for pensions are being investigated? Second, what will happen with respect to those men who are not eligible for pension, but who are trying to become reestablished in civilian life. We ought to

War Appropriation Bill
have a statement on these points, because we know that the number of men who will return and find themselves in these positions will increase. It is increasing daily.
Unless the government can give this committee a satisfactory explanation concerning their policy in this respect, we shall have a serious situation in Canada. When these men come back, are discharged and have a difficult time, it leaves a bad taste in the mouths of people across the country. It is not a good thing for those young men who are interested in entering the military services to come in contact with other men in a community who have served for a year or a year and a half, but who, upon coming back, have found it difficult to get jobs.
I am not blaming the Minister of National Defence for Air. I believe his position is quite right. No one is suggesting that the army should be responsible. Certainly, however, the government must be responsible. Unless the government is prepared to keep these men on the payroll, or unless it can set up machinery necessary to their establishment, and, if necessary, train them so that they may enter some branch of service in Canada, a difficult situation will arise. We have a responsibility to them. I hope the responsible minister will tell us, before the appropriation bill passes, just what the government proposes to do.

Perhaps the minister would permit me a word at this point. I have already concurred in the views expressed by the hon. member for Davenport. So as to indicate that the point before the committee is not purely academic, I would place before the minister one concrete instance, which is one of at least ten or more. I believe this instance will show that there is merit in the point raised.
On one occasion my attention was called by a United States citizen who lives in Detroit to the fact that when he had been in Toronto the day previous, a young boy had approached him, and said, "Can you lend me some money? I have just been discharged from the Essex Scottish regiment, which is at Camp Borden. I am a United States citizen, enlisted in the Canadian army, but because of the regulations"-which prevailed at that time- "which provide an oath of allegiance to His Majesty the King, I have forfeited my United States citizenship. I have now been discharged; I have no job; I cannot return to my own country, and I am really down and out." The gentleman who had been approached, who was anxious to do the right thing, told me where the boy could be found. I learned from him that the boy was at the
Salvation Army hostel in Toronto, and upon receipt of that information I caused him to be brought to Windsor.
This was an instance of a man separated from his wife, one who had forfeited his United States citizenship, and could not return to that country, in spite of the efforts of our immigration branch, and our Department of External Affairs. Nothing could be done because he had lost his United States citizenship. He was without funds and without a job. Had it not been for a number of people who came to his assistance he would not have been provided for until such time as he was finally able to get a job. I say without reservation that, without any thought of coddling, we owe that type of man a definite responsibility. We should have seen to it that he had work the day after he was discharged, and that every opportunity was given to him to find a job. Through the efforts of people in the community from which I come he finally found a job.
That is only one case. I bring it up, not because of any belief that the administration is not sympathetic to the problem, but rather to impress upon the committee the fact that in this respect there is a real problem.

It is perhaps unfair to ask the Minister of National Defence for Air to answer the question I have in mind, but could he ascertain for me whether the Department of Pensions and National Health has any record of the number of soldiers discharged from this war who are unemployed?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: A year or so ago I could have given the number of unemployed soldiers from the last war.

What about
this war?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I have not that information, but I would be pleased to get it-if the Minister of Pensions and National Health is not in his seat to-morrow.
The Minister of Pensions and National Health is in the chamber. Why should this problem not be dealt with now? The government is not unsympathetic.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The minister is not here; he is ill.
I thought I saw him coming in ahead of me to-night.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.

I am sure I did-unless I am labouring under a delusion. The problem is a real one. There are 18,000 men, 9,000 from overseas and 9,000 in Canada.
War Appropriation Bill

These men have been released with thirty days' pay. I have had at least ten cases in my own community of men who have been put out of the army because of a re-boarding, and their medical category did not measure up. Some of those cases are the result of pneumonia in training camps in eastern Canada. The disease left them in bad condition.
I know of one man who had a wife and eight children, and while at Aldershot he suffered from pneumonia. He was let out of the army and was given thirty days' pay. He went away, and the last I heard of him his wife did not know where he was. She was accepting charity, and she certainly put it up to me to see what could be done for her. I could not do anything but give her something.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Did he apply for a pension?

He could not be found, and as far as I know he has not yet been located. Of course, that is an extreme case.
Last fall the Minister of Pensions and National Health made a rather important statement setting out the whole position and showing that the government was giving consideration to the problem. The only criticism which I think can be made in fairness is that the government have not assumed the whole responsibility. They are assisting, but they are not assuming full responsibility. We asked these men to enlist; they have been turned back through no fault of their own, and I think it is up to this country to assume full responsibility for them until they can be reestablished in civil life. I ask the minister to give sympathetic consideration to this whole problem. It ought not to be such a problem with industry going ahead as I believe it is. Surely jobs can be found for these men. I am not prepared to-night to advocate that they should be given preference in the government war industry, because their physical condition may not be good enough. It is, however, a problem which the country might as well meet fairly and squarely.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am under the impression- and I think I am right-that the problem is being faced by this rehabilitation committee which has been set up, and it is certainly being actively considered by a committee of this house. The committee has asked for an extension of its powers in order to study the whole rehabilitation question. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) is an assiduous follower of these committees and perhaps he has more information than I.
That is correct.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: A committee of this house is actually studying this problem, as is a committee of the department. What conclusions they have arrived at up to the present, I am unable to say. I shall be glad to advise my colleague, the Minister of Pensions and National Health, of this discussion.

In the
meantime their stomachs are not filled.

The Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), who is the acting Minister of Pensions and National Health, knows how keenly I feel about this matter. There are many of these men in my riding. Our difficulty is that democracy is slow in acting. I know the sergeant-major who is looking after these fellows out at the exhibition grounds; he knows them intimately and he has told me of the difficulty there is in getting them fixed up. A man may be discharged when in need of medical attention, and the question is where he is to go.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There would be no trouble about that; he would go to Christie street.

I have had some correspondence about this matter with the Minister of National Defence as well as with the Minister of Pensions and National Health. These men are being discharged and many of them may not be pensionable. As this sergeant-major says, unless something is done we are going to make reds of these fellows. I wish to impress upon the government the necessity of speed in getting this situation cleaned up. These fellows must not be sent out with nothing to do; they must not be allowed to go on relief. It is all very well to say that a committee has been set up to study this matter, but I should like to know what the government have done about getting in touch with the various employment agencies throughout the country, particularly in Ontario. These men should be given every possible consideration. We must not make agitators out of them. We must have speed in solving this problem.
Voluntary committees may be all right, but we want more than that. Such committees are likely to let things slide and something should be done immediately to have these men placed. We do not want any injustices. I know that in my riding many of these men have developed into agitators. We do not want that sort of thing. Perhaps these men could be kept on the strength until this pension committee gets through. I understand that at the present time they are given a month's pay; is that right?

Yes.

War Appropriation Bill

If they cannot get jobs there should be some way of taking care of them in the meantime. These men are sore at being turned out. They feel that the doctors did not know what they were talking about. I cannot speak too strongly about the need for speed in getting something done in connection with these men.

Having heard what other hon. members have said about this matter, I should like to give my experience in the city of Edmonton. Just before coming to Ottawa in November, I took the trouble to get from an officer of the veterans assistance committee the number of men who had been turned out, and at that time it was forty-eight. I received the last weekly report just a few days ago and this shows that the number has increased to eighty-eight, or almost double. This officer was doing all he possibly could to place men, in either permanent or temporary jobs. He is able to place only from four to five men a week and the list continues to grow. He is trying to have some of these men placed upon the waiting list for the youth training programme in order that they may obtain some extra training to fit themselves for mechanical jobs. There seems, however, to be a hold-up there, because these men must stay on the waiting list for a considerable time. Our schools out there are doing a wonderful work in taking on these men, but they have not been able to take them on as fast as the list piles up.
I should like to associate myself with those who have spoken on this matter. No doubt this committee is trying to do something, but what are these men to do in the meantime? It has been suggested that in the coming year we shall need 300,000 more workers in factories now being built and nearing completion. I wonder what coordination there is between the Department of Pensions and National Health and the Department of Labour with a view to utilizing these men in these jobs. Possibly those departments are doing something, but it seems to me that here is where some concrete progress could be made. Surely the services of these men could be utilized in some capacity.

I should like to ask
the Minister of National Defence for Air what the policy is in connection with the establishment of training schools. A year ago the minister made it quite clear that no consideration would be given to representations by boards of trade or local organizations with regard to the selection of sites. I have before me the Melville Advance for February 20, in which is reported an interview with Pilot
Officer Cecil Bass of the Royal Air Force who was on leave from Carberry, Manitoba. The report reads:
We urged Melville to get an air port by any means possible so as to have a part in this great air development of the future. "Pull all the strings possible and get that air port somehow," he said.
I notice by the press from time to time that delegations come to Ottawa from different parts of Canada. Would the minister inform the committee what policy is followed in the selection of these sites.
And how many applications for airports he has had.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I had imagined that after three weeks of this debate, someone might get around to talking of the Department of National Defence for Air, although for a time I was under the impression that this department was going to be forgotten entirely. I had proposed to make some kind of statement on the progress of the department, indicating what we have done and what we propose to do; and in view of the fact that one must almost barge into this debate, I might as well make a statement now as at any other time. In the course of my statement I will come to the question of the selection of aerodromes, and "pulling strings," as my hon. friend puts it. I do not propose to make a formal statement at all. I know the committee is reluctant to hear such statements and I am not particularly enamoured myself of that kind of statement, but in an informal way I should like to discuss the air training plan in particular and to explain to the committee in a broad and general way just where the money which the committee is asked to vote this year-$250,000,000-is going.
As I said this afternoon in answer to a question by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), the estimates, broadly speaking, are divided into three parts. It is proposed to spend during the year 1941-42: on the home war establishment, $154,000,000; on the overseas war establishment, $15,800,000. Then there is the commonwealth air training plan, and if the committee will permit me I shall deal for the moment only with the commonwealth air training plan, being quite willing to answer in due course any questions that may be asked with reference to the other two branches of the service.
There has been a great deal of confusion in the minds of the public and of members of the house and in the press as to the air training plan. It is a huge, complex and complicated undertaking, but in a word it is this: The government of Canada is a contractor for the whole British empire to turn out-and this
War Appropriation Bill

is what I wish to emphasize-an output of air crews, consisting of pilots, gunners and observers. That is the job of work we undertook to do. All else-aerodromes, buildings, aeroplanes, trained technicians, instructors-is only-incidental to the process of doing the job we were asked to do, namely, to turn out thousands of pilots, gunners and observers, and I submit to the committee that we should be judged on the results of the job of work which we have been asked to do.
We are at the same time partners and contractors for our partners. The partners are the United Kingdom, New Zealand. Australia and Canada. We are contracting, but at the same time we are contributing, in that we contribute about 65 per cent of the joint funds and 90 per cent of the raw material, which is the young men who go into the plan and afterwards become the output, the air crews that are handed over to the Royal Air Force as members of that force. We are producing for the Royal Air Force the human units which belong to the Royal Air Force as they are graduated from our schools. I hope to make that clear to-night because I have not perhaps made it clear enough on other occasions when I have addressed the house. Our contract calls for the delivery of a certain number of human units at certain specified times.
Canada was selected from among the nations of the commonwealth to undertake this job, partly on account of our freedom from prospective attack, partly on account of our proximity to the United States, which would furnish us with a supply of raw material, and partly on account of our proximity to the United Kingdom, which would also supply us with material, and which was close enough and accessible enough to make delivery of the output easy. Fourth, I suggest that Canada was chosen because of the reputation of Canadian youth for efficiency and gallantry during the last war as members of the Royal Air Force and of the air arm of the navy.
A large part of the energies of the officers, staff and men of the Royal Canadian Air Force is devoted to this job. We might have preferred; I imagine that most of the officers of the air force would have preferred, a more direct contribution, that is to say, that we send over more all-Canadian squadrons. We were, however, asked to do this job as a matter of empire cooperation. It was believed, and I think in the event it will be proved, that the belief was founded upon common sense and reason, that by pooling the efforts of the empire to produce these young men and put them in the firing line, we would

do much better than if each part of the commonwealth endeavoured to carry on, on its own.
The minister is speaking of the work of fighting over there.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No; I say that in order to get more of these trained fighters over there, it was considered best to coordinate the efforts of the empire in this commonwealth training plan, that eventually by that means we would get more and perhaps better trained fighters over there within possibly a shorter time than would likely be the case if each part of the empire started out on its own to raise so many squadrons here and so many squadrons there. That is an entirely different set-up from the army.
Can the minister indicate how many there are now?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am not permitted to tell the committee the number of graduates from the air training plan schools.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Nor the number being trained?
I ask the minister's pardon if I embarrassed him with my question. He had stated that he wished the plan to be judged by results, and therefore I thought my question was a reasonable one.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I am very much afraid that the results will not be known until later in the war and possibly not until afterwards. In the meantime I shall endeavour to indicate to the committee as best I can just what success there has been.
In 1940 there were pre-zero arrangements. The plan itself actually started in April, 1940. It started with 168 pupils, and I remember that there were bursts of ribald laughter all across Canada at that time that we should be proposing to win the war with a schedule of 168 pupils. It was said by everyone both in the house and in the press that you could not win a war with a schedule.
What was said in the house?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I think it was said in the house, but I acquit my hon. friend of having said it. You cannot win a war with a schedule, I admit, but a schedule is an indication of study and planning, and the only way you can win a war is by studying and planning, and producing and getting the men at the right place at the right time. During the months of May and June last year, we did have a period of anxiety when it appeared evident that it would be very

War Appropriation Bill
difficult for us to get our supplies to carry on. I pass over that; it has already been discussed.
In November last I was able to tell the house that, certain classes having graduated, certain pilots and other air crew having been produced, the plan was no longer an experiment; it was a success in that we knew that we could produce. But it remained to be seen whether we could succeed in mass production. To-day I am able to say that, with 60 per cent of the plan in operation, and about ten production lines, that is series of schools, operating, we know now what we can do and we have gone in for mass production and have succeeded. Not only have we succeeded in producing what was originally intended in the plan, we have almost doubled it. Let me give figures-which do not represent the actual statistics-to illustrate my point. Supposing, when the plan was conceived and when it was started back in April, it was considered that the output on the 28th February, 1941, should be, let us say, 500 gunners, observers and pilots; not only have we achieved that figure, but we have achieved almost a thousand; to be nearer the mark, let us put it at, say, 950, because we were 5 per cent below the doubled figure which was our second target. There is a good deal of confusion about this; I do not mean that we have doubled the plan; we have simply accelerated so as to get more schools operating, more production lines, if you like, and more output at the time when, we figured, that output would be most needed; that is, now.
Has there not been a reduction in the length of the course, too?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes. I am going to explain later the reasons for that, but I am now explaining the results. I am not asking for any particular commendation or praise of us, because the results have not been achieved entirely by our own efforts. Some having been due to fortuitous circumstances; some, to change of plan by the Royal Air Force, and some, to other factors; and, as I expect to say in a moment, in some instances we accelerated and perhaps may have reached a danger point in the plan generally.
And the men themselves.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No, not the men.
I mean the calibre of the men.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No; the calibre of the men is all right.
I think the hon. member meant that the young men themselves are entitled to a meed of praise.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Oh, certainly.
That is what I meant.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Certainly, and the instructors; the members of the air force, and everyone who put his shoulder to the wheel in order to get this thing done.
I wish to make it clear that we never intended to double the plan; that is, double the number of schools, of aircraft, of output; all we did intend to do and what we have succeeded in doing was so to accelerate the output that at a given time it was almost double what it had been proposed it should be.
With all the units in operation in September, 1941, the plan will automatically flatten out and the number which it was intended to produce at that time will be produced.
Can the minister say with safety approximately what the flow will be at that time?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am not even allowed to say that. I have the figures, and would be glad to give them in confidence to my hon. friend, but I cannot say publicly what the flow will be.
I am not disagreeing with the minister.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The reason is obvious, that the lines of battle could easily be figured out if it were known how many pilots, how many gunners, how many observers were sent overseas. The enemy could then readily know how many squadrons there would be in Great Britain at a given time, and we are told that we must not give that information. I would only be too glad to do so if I could. The important thing I should like to impress upon the committee is that we have produced air crew now, and that a large number of them are overseas taking part at the present moment in the fighting over Britain.
I have in my desk a statement which I happened to read in the press two days ago, which will indicate that, even though we are not supposed to say anything about the success of the air training plan, our friends in the United Kingdom are not so chary of talking about it. In the Ottawa Journal of March 11 appears a dispatch giving an account of Sir Archibald Sinclair's statement in. the House of Commons with regard to air training and the air services generally. He said:
While Sir Charles Portal, Chief of the Air Staff, listened intently from the gallery, Sir Archibald told the cheering house men trained
War Appropriation Bill

in the commonwealth air training plan now are flying against the enemy, "and in battles this year our cause will be sustained by Canadians, Australians, New Zealanders, and men from this country, trained side by side."
That should be evidence that in Great Britain, at least, they believe we have been successful in our effort. I have here somewhere, also, a tribute-
Oh, never mind the encomiums. Give us the facts.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Apart from the dispatch
overseas of air crew, I should like to make reference in a rather guarded way, but so that the committee will know to some extent what is going on, to another feature of the work which we have been able to accomplish. We read in the press a month or so ago a statement of Air Vice-Marshal Sir Hugh Dowding, former Chief of the Air Staff of Great Britain, to the effect that night bombing was being overcome, that certain devices had been developed by the United Kingdom authorities to overcome night bombing, and that he hoped that before long they would be successful. Canadian scientists, and to some extent United States scientists, played no mean part in the further development of these devices.
I should like to mention also that men were needed to operate these devices, and it was to Canada they turned to get many of them. In November we sent more than 300 overseas, and they have been followed recently by many hundreds more. That is why we have been combing the country from one end to the other to find radio mechanics, who are being sent over for that purpose; and if any hon. members of this committee know any radio mechanic who desires to enlist and go overseas at the earliest possible moment, I should be only too glad to get his name and send him over. As a matter of fact, we have been of great assistance to the mother country in recruiting a considerable number of these young men and sending them over for the purpose of doing this important specialized work.

Will the
minister be good enough to tell the committee just what part the British technicians played in establishing the scheme? My understanding was that we were woefully scarce of technicians in Canada, and naturally so.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
In establishing the scheme
-the device? The device was invented in Britain.

I do not
mean that. I am referring to the empire air training scheme, the technical assistance given there.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I was about to say that
that was the bright side of the picture and to proceed to deal with what is not quite so bright; but before doing so I might reply to my hon. friend. I could not give offhand the number of Royal Air Force officers that are attached to the Royal Canadian Air Force for the purpose of putting this air training scheme into effect. I do not know the numbers offhand, but there have been a large number of officers-for instance, the director of medical services, Group Captain Ryan, who is a Royal Air Force officer. He was lent to us, and so was the director of training, Air Commodore Leckie. He enlisted in Canada in the last war, but he was born in Scotland, and I believe he served in the Royal Navy, fleet air arm, for many years until lent to Canada. A number of others are in the same position. They have been lent to us by the Royal Air Force to help us to put the plan into operation. I suppose the proportion would be extremely small as against the number of officers whom we have at the present time.
But at the beginning, were they not the nucleus of the training staff?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I would not say that. The nucleus of the training staff really came from the permanent force of the Royal Canadian Air Force, with such assistance as they could get from the Royal Air Force. That is the bright side of it. On the other side we have to admit, I must say, that the result, successful as it has been, has not always been brought about by orthodox methods and that the acceleration in itself has brought difficulties which we must face.
For instance, we built aerodromes faster than was required-not faster than we should have, but faster than was required by the original plan. We would have very much fewer built to-day if we had not decided to accelerate. The result was undoubtedly that the cost was higher. When we decided to accelerate last spring-and, as was said to-day, everyone was for speed and more speed- the emphasis was not on economy, I will say quite plainly to the committee, so far as the air training scheme and the putting up of our schools and the development of aerodromes were concerned the emphasis was on getting them built as fast as we could in order to put pupils into them and have those pupils turned

War Appropriation Bill
out. The result was a higher cost and, I should say, greater confusion probably; that expansion of itself disorganized the steady expansion which was planned, and caused us a great deal of trouble.
Another factor in the acceleration was the shortening of the training period, as my hon. friend has pointed out. That was as a result of consultation with the United Kingdom authorities. It has, however, the effect of transferring certain of the more advanced training to a position nearer to the theatre of actual war. It does not bring the pilot out, in many instances-it refers only to pilots-very much earlier than would have been accomplished under the old system we were following, but it does send him overseas where he completes his training in operational work a little earlier than he otherwise would.
There is another factor in the acceleration- what is called "overbearing." We took a certain number of pupils into a school at one time; and after consultation we found, particularly in the elementary schools, that with the establishment, both in aircraft and in instructors, it was quite possible and quite easy to train more pupils than were originally allowed to these elementary training schools. We increased the number in the proportion of four to five. This to some extent placed a greater burden on the instructors and required also the building of additional accommodation for the extra pupils we took in, at greater cost.
There was another factor. We wanted to get aircraft more quickly. That placed on the shoulders of the Minister of Munitions and Supply a burden which became pretty heavy for him to bear. It is easy for me to say, "Open a school six weeks, or two months or three months earlier than it was planned to be opened." We can get the building erected and we can scurry around and get instructors, but it is left to the Minister of Munitions and Supply to find the aircraft. He has had considerable trouble over that, and I wish to pay him this tribute, that so far he has not complained very much about the burden put upon him.
Then there are real dangers, which we hope to be able to deal with, in this acceleration itself. Aircraft, like any other machines, need overhauling. At the present time most of the aircraft we have are new and we are using up our capital. We are using these aircraft as hard and as fast as we can. In normal times, if this were not war time, I would say that the leader of the opposition could rise in his place and accuse me of the most reckless extravagance and improvidence.
Not you.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Not me, no. As a matter of fact, we are using up that capital. These aircraft, after a certain period of time, need overhauling. They cannot keep on running eternally and the time will come-I wish to make this danger plain to the committee- when we shall have too many needing to be overhauled at the same time. This will not bog down or stop the plan, but it may retard it to some extent. I say frankly, I have no alibi if that happens, but we know there is that danger.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will lack of overhauling mean casualties?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No; but the planes will be grounded. They will be unserviceable. I understand it varies with different types; but with certain types, after they have gone 360 hours, they must be taken down for overhauling. If the work is something of a minor nature it can be carried out at the station and might take a week or so; but if it is something major-from 360 to 400 hours- it may take a month in order that every part of the machine may be gone over so as to make it thoroughly safe.
Is provision being made for that now?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; in the estimates there is something like S19,000,000 for that kind of overhaul at contractors', apart from the ordinary maintenance overhaul which we have at the stations themselves.
Would the minister give the break-down of that 3250,000,000.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will later on. This overhaul not only means that the contractors must have efficient men, but it also means-and there is our greatest difficulty-that we must have spares. Spare parts are really our greatest difficulty at the present time. That arises from the extreme desire of all manufacturers to produce the completed article; they are not very much interested in making spare parts, they want to be able to say, we have turned out so many aircraft. The result of that is that we have a large number of aircraft which at the present time are down and unserviceable for lack of comparatively small spares. We are endeavouring to have these spares manufactured in Canada as far as we can.
Is that for the primary trainers or the advanced?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I am speaking of the plan as a whole. There is not so much difficulty with the primary trainers, because they are manufactured in Canada, but the advanced
War Appropriation Bill

trainers come from either the United States or Great Britain. I do not think I am saying anything derogatory to the effort Great Britain is making; in fact, I am astounded that they are able to ship their spares in such an orderly fashion as they do. It would not be astonishing to find them just jumbled into boxes and shipped, but in fact they are shipped in pretty good order. At the same time there is, in many instances, a lack of comparatively unimportant spares.

Is that not a very strong
argument for subcontractors for these parts?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We are endeavouring to have these parts made here as far as it is at all possible so that we shall not have that difficulty. We are even going beyond that; we are endeavouring to have them made in our own shops, hand made; it takes longer perhaps, but not as long as trying to get them from the other side or the United States.
As I say, this is a serious danger. As far as we have been able to estimate we do not believe that the plan will ever go beyond 15 per cent less than the target output; we might perhaps go 20 per cent below if we were so unfortunate as to have a very large number of our aircraft down at the same time for lack of spares. In order to meet that difficulty the deputy minister, Mr. de Carteret, has asked Mr. Colbrook, who came to the department some six months ago from the Robert Simpson company, Toronto, to be the trouble shooter and take special charge of this job of seeing, first, that the overhaul work is carried out by the contractors, and, second, to rush the spares as fast as possible. We think we can overcome that obstacle, but it is a serious one in the way of continuous output.
It might be interesting to the committee, and I do not know that it will give very much information to the enemy, to have some idea of the present situation with regard to aircraft. Let me say, first, that when the plan is complete-and it is a three-year plan-in April, 1943, we shall have put through the plan 6,100 aircraft, and I am making allowance for wastage; we shall have something over 6,000 aircraft-I speak now only of the training planes.
We have at the present moment something like 2,400 aircraft of all types. I can give the percentages of aircraft at the different types of schools. When I speak in percentages I speak not only of what is called the initial establishment but also of the "in reserve". We have in our elementary schools 100-9 per cent of planes, so there is no difficulty there. The service flying training schools are of two

kinds, one which uses twin engines and the other which uses single engines. As far as the twin-engine schools are concerned we are short of aircraft; we have 46 per cent of what we should have. As far as the single engine schools are concerned we have 89 per cent of what we require, which is reasonably good; it means that our reserve is not up to what it should be, but we have all we want for the initial establishment.
What kind are the single engine planes and what the twin-engine planes?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The twin engines would be Ansons and Cessna. The single would be Harvards largely. The schools are equally divided at the present time, five service flying training schools using single engines and five using twin engines. In the air observer schools we have 70 per cent of our requirements. They are twin-engine Ansons. For the bombing and gunnery schools we have 86 per cent. For the air navigation schools, which need a very small number of twin-engine aircraft, we have 44 per cent and we can soon catch up. For the wireless training schools, singleengine aircraft, we have 82 per cent.
With respect to the Ansons, we never expected to get them until April. We did, however, expect to do better with what is known as the Fort Fleet 60, which is being made or assembled by a private manufacturer in Canada, because it carries an American Jacobs engine. We expected to get that in December, or January at the latest, but at the present time we have a promise that we shall receive production at the end of March. In order to overcome that difficulty, which was to some extent foreseen, Mr. Ralph Bell and Mr. Duncan, the former deputy minister, in July or August went to the United States and purchased a very large number of twin-engine Cessnas, which are now beginning to arrive, and I am told by our training officers that they are an excellent machine and will in every respect not only replace but probably be better than the Ansons. There was a little delay in the arrival of these Cessnas some time in January, and it gave us cause for some concern, but the production now is coming along very well and will fill the gap for some little time to come.
I do not want to enter into the controversy which has been stirred up in the press with respect to the power and authority which should be conferred on the proposed minister of aircraft production, or on the suggestion made that this minister should control all the engineering. It is a long, long controversy which has taken place probably in every business, as to whether the man who uses the article-in this case it is a plane-should have

War Appropriation Bill
something to do with the design of it, or whether he should give his orders for the plane, fold his arms and let the thing be built for him.
Speaking without any authority, with the exception of what I have read, I have learned that the German system prior to the war was to establish a model and to go ahead and produce it on mass production lines. On the other hand, I learn that the British went in for developing better and better aircraft. The result was that they had fewer of them, but the result was also that they had the Spitfire and the Hurricane when the time came.
I do not wish to take one side or the other in that controversy, but I do say that the aircraft production side may have grounds for saying that to some extent they have been delayed by the engineering side in the Royal Canadian Air Force. The engineers and the operators of the machines-the people who fly them-are constantly looking for the newest improvements. There is no doubt about that. There is the tendency on both sides to carry out their ideas. The producer wants to put the thing on the production line, and get it off. He does not want any change. The man who is going to use it does want change. As I said, I am not going to take one side or the other, but I think the committee is entitled to the statement that there are two sides to the story, and that either side can make a pretty good cause.
I have given what I thought was the good side of the picture. Then I pointed out the difficulties in production. I should now like to refer to what I describe as the headaches.
Headaches?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes, headaches. The house and country has quite a legitimate concern in all matters connected with the air training scheme, and particularly as it affects individuals and as it affects different sections of the country. But I would say and repeat that our job is to produce air crews, and we must take every possible means we can to get on with the production. It is just too bad sometimes if some hon. member does not get an aerodrome in his constituency, but I am not going to stop the plan to discuss the matter with him. I suggest to the committee that this is as good a time as any for them to have a bargain day, and for all of them to rise in their places and tell me how well suited are their particular constituencies to accommodate the building of aerodromes. There is the one who claims that there should be an aerodrome in his constituency because the people in it are more loyal than the people in any other part of Canada. There is the other person
who claims that there should be one in his constituency, because it would help to keep the disloyal element down. I would like to take in both sides.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Too late for that now.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
That is one headache. There is a further headache, and perhaps one more difficult of solution. Perhaps it does not affect individual members, but it does affect those of us who are operating the plan. I refer to the matter of recruiting. Perhaps hon. members will bear with me if I outline some of the difficulties in connection with recruiting.
At the beginning of the war thousands of young men desired to join the air force, and we were obliged to put them off. We could not take them all in. There was no room for them, either in the training schools which trained the technicians, or at other points. When I refer to training schools I have in mind schools like that at St. Thomas. May I add, in passing, that we now have about
6,000	technicians in training at St. Thomas and other places, and we have actually trained and brought into the force 10,000 trained mechanics.
If those young men were mechanics before they joined the force, there was very little difficulty in bringing them in. But if they were not mechanics, they were difficult to handle because we had to open schools for them. If they intended to become air crews- and that includes pilots, gunners and observers -it was still more difficult because, up until April we really had no schools for them. At that time the schools began, but very slowly.
We were considerably worried as to what we should do. I believe it was last May or June that I announced in the house that rather than see these young men go around kicking their heels while waiting, we would take them in and give them three months' drill. We did that. We took in 5,000, and gave them the drill. Those young fellows are now in the plan, and are being turned out as air crews.
But our difficulty is this: I do not mind saying to the committee that we will require thousands and thousands of air crews. Those young men represent the very flower of the youth of our country. They must be A-plus physically, and they must have educational qualifications equivalent to matriculation from high school. In order to give some idea of the problem, I might refer to some figures which, I believe, were placed on record by my colleague the Minister of National Defence. I refer to the number of young men of the age of twenty-one years. There will be for
War Appropriation Bill

training this year 93,000 young men of the age of twenty-one years. Without hesitation one can knock off 33 per cent of those as being unfit even for military training camps. That is, they would be placed in classes C-l or C, and unfit to walk five miles. They are completely eliminated, so far as the air force is concerned. Then, the difference between C and A-plus, with good eyesight, would mean that one would knock off another 30,000, leaving about 30,000 annually from which we can draw.
Then, if one looks at them from the point of view of educational qualifications I believe he would knock off another half of those- these would be the ones who have not high school matriculation-leaving 15,000 eligibles. Laying aside figures which I have, but which apparently do not fit the picture any better, we find that in all provinces, with the exception of Quebec, there are 119,000 young men in secondary schools, and approximately 30,000 in Quebec. I give the two figures, because the school systems are not the same. This makes a total of about 150,000 in all schools. But I take it they would be in three or four age groups, and I have not been able to arrive at an accurate yearly figure. But the figure I have taken is that of the young men of twenty-one years. Therefore, that leaves me for the air force approximately 15,000 men a year. The year brackets are from eighteen years to twenty-eight years, and we are not particularly keen on accepting anyone over twenty-five years. Therefore the pool from which we can draw consists of about 105,000; and there are, let us say, 15,000 or 20,000 more coming in every year.
We will need thousands of these young men. I do not want to say how many thousands a month, but we will need thousands a month. We do not need them all yet. I have in hand a reserve of about six months, but we do not want to let them get away from us, if it is possible. That is our problem.
What we are doing at this time is to let them come to our recruiting offices. We enlist them, and let them go away on leave without pay. We tell them to come back in July or August. We say to them, "Do not give up your jobs; do not give up your schooling; we will require you; we will tell you to report in July or August; the day on which we tell you to report will be the day you will report, and there will be no further postponement."
The difficulty up to the present time has been that we could not tell a man when he was coming in, because we did not know exactly how our plan was getting along. But we do know now, with some degree of cer-

tainty. We are able to say that a certain number of men shall come in every month, or on such and such a date.

Have they had their
medical examinations?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We are going to enlist
them, pass them through their medical, put them in the air force, let them go away without pay, and tell them to come back in three or four months. At the present time I have in hand about five or six months' supply. We would want at least three months' supply ahead, so that at the end of about three months from now we would be taking in some of the men who come before us to-day and who are sent away on leave. That is the only way I can think of whereby we can hold these young men. They are going to be extremely precious to us. I do not want the committee to get the idea that I am starting an intensive recruiting campaign. We are not doing that because the time is not ripe yet. We do not want our recruiting offices to be thronged with young men at the present time. Our present plan calls for a certain number of students to go into each school each month and we cannot take any more unless we expand the plan. The plan may be expanded, but at the moment it has not been decided to do so.

The minister said a few moments ago that there would be 15,000 of the twenty-one year age group; he then mentioned the group from eighteen to twenty-eight years and I understood him to say there were 105,000 in that group.
Mr. POW'ER: I said that I was not particularly anxious to have the twenty-five to twenty-eight group; I would rather have them under twenty-five years. Seven times 15,000 makes 105,000, but the ten-year bracket would give you 150,000.
Will the recruits who have been examined and who are to come back in July be given another medical examination?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I would expect that they will be.
If a man does not pass the second examination, will he be eligible for pension?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
They must be good men to be passed. I would say that point will come up in the pension committee, as to whether the disability which a man might incur during the time he is absent on leave without pay would be pensionable. I leave that to the good judgment of the members of the pension

War Appropriation Bill
committee to decide. Offhand, I would say, "no", but that will be something for them to decide.
What matriculation standard is required?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: High school.
In each province?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: In the province in which a man applies.

Is any arrangement made to transfer men from other forces to the air force after they have enlisted? Many young men who applied for the air force have since enlisted in the other forces and some of them are anxious to get back in the air force.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Churchill calls that combing the mane to sharpen the tooth. I am strongly in favour of it. If we are ever stuck for recruits, I think we shall go to the army to get them. I think we shall be able to get quite a number who would be fully qualified. My colleague says that he is not so keen on my taking men from the navy. It may be that the supply will be exhausted sooner than we expect.

There are many young men who are actively engaged in England at the present time and who would like to get into the air force. I have in mind a young fellow who has been over there for seven months. Before he left he tried to, get into the air force and he was given the assurance that the transfer could be made. When he got to England he attempted to get a transfer from the artillery into the air force, but he was told that no provision had been made for such a transfer. He was advised that plans were under discussion and they thought that within a short time he would be given a transfer. Has anything been done to take care of such cases?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Plans were brought before me during the last two or three weeks whereby Canadians serving in England might be transferred to the air force if they were found to be qualified. I am not sure of the details, but the principle has been accepted.
It has not been completed.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I cannot say whether the appropriate cables have been exchanged.
That principle was in effect during the last war when Canadian lieutenants were transferred to the Royal Air Force.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not mind telling the committee that some difficulty may arise on account of the set-up of our air training plan. That plan calls for everyone to go in as a private. There might be some difficulty in having men come into the plan who have commissions in other services. That is really one reason why I am dodging it for the moment. I understand it is being done in England without any difficulty, but there may be some trouble here. Under our plan young men who may be able to qualify for commissions in the army join as members of the air crew in order to go through the six months' course and be commissioned in the air force. They might feel that they had not been treated fairly if someone else came in direct from the army with a commission. That is something that must be ironed out.
Will the minister give the committee a break-down of the 1941-42 expenditure of S394 million, referred to on page 1494 of Hansardf

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
May I finish with my headaches first? I just want to enumerate them because I know every member of the committee has some knowledge of some of them. I simply want hon. members to know that I am fully aware of them.
The next thing is the selection of air crew and the granting of commissions. There has been a slight change, but originally all young men who wished to be air crew went into the initial training school after going through the manning depot and the security guards, if necessary.

Is the
selection left to the man himself, or is that made by the selection committee?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
That is where I am coming to the trouble. The vast majority of the young men want to be pilots as there is more glamour in that branch of the service. It must be remembered that the whole set-up is based upon the Royal Air Force, to which these men are consigned after we graduate them. Fifty per cent of the pilots receive commissions, thirty-three per cent here upon graduation and seventeen per cent within a few months. The same thing is true with respect to observers; but with respect to gunners, few if any receive commissions until they have proved themselves in actual fighting at the front. As a result of representations made here, the United Kingdom has recently agreed to give commissions to two per cent of those graduating as air gunners.
But here is the difficulty. Assume we have three young men with equal attainments, possessing the same educational qualifications
War Appropriation Bill

and physical standards. They enter the initial training school where the selection is made. After a month or six weeks one is told that he will be a pilot, another that he will be an observer and the third poor devil is told that he will be a gunner. For six months he must study wireless at the wireless school. It is very difficult to explain to the boys and the parents just why this is. I must say that the men in charge of these schools are of the highest calibre, but I have always had some doubt personally as to -whether one young man can be sufficiently observed among 600 in a short space of time to decide whether he shall be a pilot, an observer or a gunner. But that has been the way it has been worked, and it has given us more trouble than anything else.
I can give some instances. A son of a very great friend of mine, a judge in one of the provinces-if I am not mistaken he is the chief justice-came from the university to join up as air crew. After a certain time he was told that he would never make a pilot, that he would never make an observer, but that he had to be a gunner.
