The son was naturally very much disappointed and his father wrote to me, but I could not do anything about the matter.
Another case was that of the son of a very great friend of mine, a former associate in matters connected with pensions, veterans' problems and so forth. This young man also had had a university training, but he was told that he had to be a gunner. His father was very much upset because he had intended the boy to try for a commission in the infantry, but the boy wanted to be a pilot. Unfortunately he did not qualify. And so on all down the line.
I could tell the committee of an amusing case. An old friend of mine came to me and said, "My boy must have been made a gunner, I think, on account of his name". The family name was not MacDonald or MacPherson or Macintosh, but they were descendants of people who had been kings in their own land many years ago. I asked, "What is wrong with his name?" He replied, "His first two names are Roger Casement, but little did I know when I christened him that he would be fighting against those devils some day". He had suspected that because his name was Roger Casement he had not been appointed1 a pilot.
This just illustrates one of our great difficulties. We have lowered the standard of education for gunners, and there is the odd chance of two per cent getting commissions. But even though the chances of a commission are the same for observers as for pilots, the young men always insist on trying to be

pilots. We have endeavoured to the best of our ability to show them that observers perform just as essential work as pilots-as a matter of fact the observer course is harder -and work that is just as useful, but in the public imagination the pilot is the man. Members of parliament have written to me to see what can be done about such and such a boy and I have always said that I do not dare to interfere. Members of the committee will readily understand that if I interfered in one case I would bring down on my shoulders the burden of choosing vocations for thousands of young men, and I am not going to do that.
Then there is the security guards policy, to which I referred a moment ago, the policy of keeping these young men in reserve. We send them out as guards for aerodromes. It is pretty hard on the young man who thinks he is going to join the air force and that within a week or two he will be riding the skies, to have to be sent to Yarmouth or Prince Rupert or somewhere else to form fours. He does not like it, of course. But we were obliged to adopt that policy in order to keep them in reserve. We are trying to get away from that policy as much as possible, but we still want to have available at least
3,000	to 4,000 of these young men whom we can bring in readily if there is any failure among those who have enlisted and may not turn out on time. We must keep a large reserve on hand to keep on feeding our schools. I have had complaints from members and parents about this, but there is nothing else to be done, and we are doing the best we can under the circumstances.
The only other point I might refer to is the cost of aerodromes, perhaps not excessive, but expenses have been incurred that we might not have incurred had we not been in such a hurry. I mention all these matters not to preclude any discussion of them because they are things which it is essential the committee should take cognizance of. I mention them merely to show that we are aware of these difficulties, and are endeavouring to solve them. Some, of course, we shall never be able to solve. We are keeping our mind and bending all our energies towards one thing, the turning-out of air crews as well trained and as fast as we can, to go overseas to take part in the fighting there. All the rest, as I said before, is incidental to that main purpose. These other matters are of importance, of course, but the primary and paramount thing is to send our young men overseas to man the aircraft for Britain to carry on the battle, and that is what we are trying to do.

The minister may have already answered this question in the course of his remarks, but I am not just clear what the situation is. speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I should think that a wireless operator, ground, would not be used much overseas and would probably be sent to one of our home stations.
That is where he is now.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If my hon. friend, will write me, I will check up on it.

Do British pilots, when they are in Canada, receive Canadian pay or are they still under British pay? I refer to the ones who have come here under the air training plan. The reason why I ask is that some of them who are in western Ontario have their wives with them, and I believe they find it a little difficult to carry on. I wondered what scale of pay and allowances they are receiving.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is confusing two things. There are some who are attached to the air training plan, and they are under our own pay and allowances. Others are out at a special school; they are under a different system, altogether, and they are not and may never be under the joint air training plan. They are carried directly on the strength of the Royal Air Force and to all intents and purposes are Royal Air Force personnel.

Thank you. There is just one other point. In the course of his remarks the minister said he did not intend to get into a controversy with respect to air service control. I do not want to start one, but I believe he suggested that those people who are flying machines and so on should have quite a say in what is going

TVar Appropriation Bill

on. They should no doubt present their information and express their wishes to the engineering branch in his own department, the Royal Canadian Air Force. The minister suggested that his own department may have been responsible for certain delays on account of changes. I realize that and quite appreciate it, but what I have tried to advocate is the establishment of a ministry of air production, also the very thing which he pointed out, that his own engineering branch which are in close cooperation with his operators should be at all times in control of and in touch with that ministry of air production so that we shall not have a repetition of the difficulties and delays which we have had in the past. That is what we have been advocating. I do not want to enter into any controversy, but I wish to make my position clear.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The question is not whether they should be in touch-they are in touch- but, should they be controlled by a production ministry? I said I did not wish to get into that controversy. It is something with regal'd to which I am willing to listen to anybody's advice. Frankly, I do not know, and I am giving the two sides of the story as I understand it.

I understand that it has been the policy of the department, in order to avoid any international complications, that no air fields be established on the prairies south of the main line of railway. I wonder whether that still prevails.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That never was a definite policy of the department. I do not mind saying that there was one place where an aerodrome might have been established had it not been thought at that time that it might involve international complications, since the proposed landing field was extremely close to the border, and the flyers in taking off every day would have been almost obliged to cross the border. That situation arose six or eight months ago. I do not know that the question arises at the moment. As a matter of fact, there is a school at Windsor.
The best in Canada.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Also one has been established at Boundary Bay, which is extremely close to the international border. My hon. friends from British Columbia can tell me the distance; it cannot be more than five or six miles from the border.
Two miles.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will have to make a speech to explain this. I will read the agreement covering the training of aircraft crews and pilots in Canada and their subsequent service, which was entered into between Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand. There is one section which. I believe, will make clear to hon. members just what we are driving at.

Is this the commonwealth air training plan?

War Appropriation Bill

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes. Article 15 is probably the one in point:
The United Kingdom government undertakes that pupils of Canada, Australia and New Zealand shall, after training is completed, be identified with their respective dominions, either by the method of organizing dominion units and formations or in some other way, such methods to be agreed upon with the respective dominion governments concerned. The United Kingdom government will initiate intergovernmental discussion to this end.
Article 16:
The government of the United Kingdom will, subject to the provisions of Article 17, provide the pay, allowances, pensions and other noneffective benefits, maintenance and other expenses of the pilots and aircraft crews who are trained in Canada (other than those made available for service with the Royal Canadian Air Force in accordance with the provisions of Article 14)-[DOT]
I may say that article 14 permitted Canada to keep for home defence a certain number, a comparatively small number, of pilots.
-with effect from the dates of their embarkation in Canada for service with, or in conjunction with, the Royal Air Force.
That means that the British government is responsible for the pay and allowances of these graduates from the moment they get on the boat to leave Canada.
The government of the United Kingdom also undertakes to arrange for those pupils who are made available for service with, or in conjunction with, the Royal Air Force to be embarked as speedily as possible after the completion of their training, and to defray the cost of their passage to the stations to which they are appointed on leaving Canada.
With respect to Canadians and British rates of pay:
The pay, allowances, pensions and other non-effective benefits, maintenance and other expenses, for which the government of the United Kingdom undertakes liability under the provisions of article 16-
Which I have just read.
-will be as laid down in Royal Air Force regulations.
If it should be decided by the government of Canada, the government of Australia or the government of New Zealand to supplement the amount so issued, any such supplement will be borne by the government concerned.
The Dominion of Canada does pay to each one of these, during all the time he is abroad, the difference in his rate of pay. During the time he is here he gets Canadian rates of pay. From the moment he embarks he gets the British rate of pay, but the government of Canada undertakes to make up the difference between the British and the Canadian rate.

That is what the $15,000,000 is for?
14873-102J

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, and for three squadrons that are overseas.

speechtext: We pay pensions also.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
It would certainly run

You pay the difference in

In other words, they are

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes. That is the status of
these pilots. In the air training plan we have expended so much money-65 per cent of the plan-and then the pilots go over and are at the disposal of the Royal Air Force; but, as I read a moment ago, it was decided at the time of the agreement that some means should be found of identifying Canadian pilots either bj' unit or by formation or in some other way. It did not stand to reason that thousands of our young men should go there and have no connection with Canada, being spread all over Libya, Greece, Ethiopia and everywhere else. Therefore one of the errands of which the Minister of National Defence spoke was the endeavour to bring into practical application clause 16, which says that they should be identified. As a result of this, arrangements have been made whereby twenty-five squadrons will be set up as Royal Canadian Air Force squadrons. Mind you, they will be paid at British rates of pay. They will be maintained as British, because they do belong to the British, but they will be called Canadian squadrons because they will be all Canadian pupils. As to the dates at which they were formed, I had better not mention that.
The consultations took place during the summer. When the Minister of National Defence went overseas he was asked by the government to undertake this task of settling the question of identification, and the agreement was signed by him, with the Right Hon. Sir Archibald Sinclair, Minister of Air. It provides that there shall be twenty-five squadrons called Canadian squadrons, from graduates of the joint air training plan, to-be formed at different dates which I will not specify, and that all the Canadian pilots and
War Appropriation Bill

air crews from the air training plan-not in the Royal Canadian Air Force units or formations, because there would be many more than twenty-five squadrons, which represent *only about one-fifth of the output within the next few months, but all those who were mot in these squadrons-would continue to wear the Canadian air force uniforms and Canada badges. This arrangement is to be revised in September, 1941. It goes on to say:
6. Under the air training plan and at the request of the United Kingdom government, the Royal Canadian Air Force has concentrated on the production of pilots and air crews. This has necessitated the provision and employment in Canada of ground personnel who would otherwise have been available for service with Royal Canadian Air Force squadrons overseas. It is recognized, however, as desirable, so far as it may mutually be considered practicable, that the United Kingdom ground personnel who, for the reason stated above, will be required for the squadrons referred to in paragraph 2 should gradually be exchanged for Royal Canadian Air Force ground personnel employed on the air training plan, with a view to achieving homogeneity of personnel in these squadrons.
The ground crew of these squadrons will be United Kingdom for the moment, because we are using all the ground crew we can possibly find for the training plan in Canada. The suggestion is that there should be exchanges. Possibly it will be that when we have trained enough, we shall be able to send some of our young men overseas to serve as ground crew.
Strictly speaking, the operations of the Royal Canadian Air Force as such are confined to Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No. We have three Royal Canadian Air Force squadrons of our own overseas, and have had for several months. They are equipped, maintained and manned, as to both ground and air, by Canada.
And paid by Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes. I may add that we are now on a kind of flat rate. At first we made an arrangement to pay for replacement every time an aircraft was destroyed, but it complicated bookkeeping to a considerable extent, and we had to put a large amount of money in the estimates last year on the assumption that there would be a one hundred per cent renewal every month. We have now an arrangement with the British government whereby they will supply aircraft for any destroyed, and will feed our men, on a flat rate. We pay something like three million dollars a year for a squadron, and they take chances whether the squadron will be continuously occupied or not. We pay the same

flat rate no matter how many or how few aircraft are destroyed. It is called a capitation rate. The same applies to feeding.
These three squadrons will operate on a different basis to the twenty-five?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; they are entirely Canadian, just as Canadian as the army is over there, whereas the other squadrons are composed of Canadians who graduated from the plan but are on initial rate of pay from the British, having been formed for purposes of identification.
Are these army cooperation squadrons?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Some will be army cooperation; some, bombers and some, fighters. The rest of the agreement deals with the fact that at the beginning there may be a shortage of senior Canadian officers to fill the posts of squadron commanders, because they will be graduates from the plan and will not have the experience. At the inception the United Kingdom personnel will be in command of these young men, but as we go on, Canadians will replace them so that the squadrons will become entirely Canadian. Then there is provision for consultation as between the air officer commanding Canadian overseas headquarters and senior officers in the air force, and also the British, with regard to the employment of these squadrons-when they are to be used in any major operation.

I wish to ask the minister a question and he can use his discretion about answering it. speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not think any have flown in them, certainly not in the air training plan. The only ones who would fly in that plane would be skilled pilots who had graduated. It is not a training plane; the big one is a good transport plane, and there is a fighter plane but it is not being used by any pupils.

It was the fighter plane to which I had reference. They were trained pilots who were using it, and I heard some complaint that the Canadian assembled plane was not a particularly safe

one; there was that feeling. Therefore I wanted to ask the minister whether these accidents had been more prevalent with any one type of plane.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No. The other day I was referring only to accidents in training. There have been very few accidents in the home war establishment, the defence forces, although there have been some. I do not remember having had statistics made out for this, but they are not more prevalent with any one type than another, certainly not in the air training plan.
Early in his statement the minister referred to 90 per cent of those in the air training plan being Canadians.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The pupils, yes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

They must have an air training plan quite apart from this.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Most of their elementary training men come through the training schools here. They have an air force of their own and presumably many of their men go direct. I do not, however, think they have a large air training scheme of their own.
Have we any appropriation to cover the construction of the proposed Alaska project?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes, in the home war
appropriation.
Can the minister give us any information in that connection?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Simply that we are spending about eight or nine million dollars on station facilities in the interior of British Columbia to Alaska. I should not like to give the break-down any further than that. But I should be glad to give my hon. friend the information personally if he will come to my office. It is a defence project.
Is this just for the purpose of providing air fields in that area?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Staging facilities.

I understand that after the last war an officers' reserve list was set up. It was necessary for an officer to keep himself in good standing from year to year. I know several of these men, approximately forty-five years of age, who have kept in good standing, passed medical tests A-l, but apparently they cannot get beyond that point. Some of them have taken several of these medicals in the course of a -year. I have been asked by some of them to find out what the advantages are
o.e. having kept in good standing on the reserve list and to secure information regarding the method of absorbing these men into active service at this time.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If my hon. friend is speaking of the air force, obviously a man of forty-five would not be any use to us as a flyer, no matter how good his state of health; we are not taking them in at forty-five now. But we have been taking in, I might say, hundreds of men who served in the last war and have a good record as administrative ground officers. We have been taking them in up to fifty years of age as ground officers.
I understand these men have applied for appointments as Link trainers or ferry pilots. I was not referring to active service in the air.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We are taking them in
every day. Of course there is a background of about two thousand men who are extremely eager to serve their country at about $2,500 to $3,000 a year in a nice soft job at home wearing a uniform.
With a brass hat.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
With a brass hat, and they are extremely indignant-I am not referring to the gentleman my friend speaks of-when they are told "Well, you have not been selected yet." There is a selection board that selects from among the applicants those who, we think, would make administrative officers or accountants or engineer officers, and when they are not selected they write to me or to their member wondering why we refuse to let them serve their country. We cannot take them all in, w:e must make a selection amongst those many thousands. As far as I know, we are selecting former air officers for administrative positions whenever any of them are qualified. I have insisted right along that former air officers particularly get the preference for administrative positions when they are otherwise qualified.
War Appropriation Bill

speechtext: There may be some exceptions but the limit is fifty. There may be an odd exception, I do not remember any; a person over fifty is barred.

speechtext:
That is another thing I
am not supposed to give, but I think we should give it. I do not agree with all my officers about the hush-hush policy. I do not see any reason why we should not tell the country how many people are in the air force.
I have here the last weekly report: officers, 3,490; airmen, 42,732.

That does not include
the empire air training scheme.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; that is everyone serving now in Canada. That includes students and all kinds in the scheme.

That does not
include the Royal Air Force men?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
No, except those who are
attached to us or loaned to us specially. That in terms of the last war is about three divisions; when we talk of raising so many divisions of infantry, let it be remembered that there are three divisions of airmen in this country at the present time.

About what proportion in
the commonwealth air training scheme are Canadians?

speechtext:
Ninety per cent of the

Some four to five hundred United States trained flyers have been enlisted or commissioned in the air force as instructors. Without them we would have had an extremely difficult time to get as far as we have.
We have the best neighbours in the w'orld.
What is the percentage of Americans in the air force?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I would say at the moment between 7 per cent and 10 per cent of the air crews; that is, those pupils who will be graduated. To a large extent these are Americans who have come to and are serving in Canada.

If questions concerning
the air programme are exhausted, I should like to ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply a question. If, however, other hon. members wish to ask questions of the Minister of National Defence for Air, I shall delay my question.
Is the Department of National Defence for Air, as such, responsible for the selection geographically of the various air training fields, or is that the responsibility of some other department?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Shortly after my appointment I explained the system of selection. The Department of Transport makes a general survey of prospective aerodromes across Canada. It then makes a report to what is known as the aerodrome development committee, which is composed of officers of the Department of Transport and of the Department of National Defence for Air. They then decide what aerodrome is to be developed, and where aerodromes are to be located. The report then comes to the minister, and the minister says "yes" to whatever they tell him, because he is not going to get mixed up in aerodrome development or the selection of aerodromes, because he has something else to do.

What is the policy of the government with respect to the location of aerodromes and air training fields? What are the guiding principles? I can understand that naval training would be carried on at the seaboard, and that other branches of the service would be carried out where natural facilities are available. I should like now to know the guiding principle which prompts the government to locate air fields for example at Ottawa, Montreal, Northern Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces. Is it the principle of proximity to population, or what are the determining factors?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
On the fii'st or second day after I came to the department I made a statement to the house, received from one of

War Appropriation Bill
the officers in the department, in which I indicated the guiding principles. The first principle is to get a place suitable for development as an aerodrome. Then, at the time these selections are made there was an attempt to foster recruiting, and in order to help recruiting, the aerodromes were spread at suitable locations across Canada. As has already been explained, there was at that time a tendency not to place aerodromes too close to the United States border. There was some thought that on account of climatic conditions, including heavy snowfalls and the like, some sections of the country would not be as suitable as others for the development of aerodromes. All these principles, however, were laid down.
I have sent for a copy of Hansard, and I should be pleased to read again what I read last year. Generally speaking, however, the principle followed when placing an aerodrome at any point is that such point has been found to be a suitable location.
How does the department decide that it is a suitable location?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is the decision of the Department of Transport in conjunction with officers of my department.

All bon. members have
listened with keen interest to what I would term a straightforward statement made by the Minister of National Defence for Air this evening. Had we heard similar statements earlier from other ministers, we would have been through long ago.
That is quite a comment.

I have not held up the committee very much. I would ask the minister who has interjected that I should have liked to ask him many questions, but possibly I was rather intimidated by the replies he gave to some other hon. members. I am now asking the question of the Minister of National Defence for Air as to whether or not he can give us information respecting the number of aerodromes and training centres in Saskatchewan. Are there one or two there operated solely by the Royal Air Force?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

Could the minister give
us some information on that point? Are there others operated jointly, and what is the expenditure by this government and by the British government in that connection?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend be
satisfied if I answered him respecting the aerodromes in Saskatchewan operated by the Royal Canadian Air Force, and let him find out the answer to his question?
I should like to have the ones operated by the Royal Air Force, alone.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I would rather tell him
those operated by the Royal Canadian Air Force. My answer would give the same result, and my conscience would be clear in that I had not mentioned the location of Royal Air Force schools in Canada.

That is spoiling the
minister's record.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: My colleague suggests that I should have kept up my record for being straightforward. In Saskatchewan there is an elementary school and also an air observer school at Prince Albert. There is an elementary school and an air observer school at Regina. Then there are Canadian schools at Mossbank, Dafoe, Saskatoon, and Yorkton Those would appear to be all the Canadian flying schools in Saskatchewan. Then, as my hon. friend knows, there is a munitions training school at Regina, and several other ground schools. I believe, however, he was referring only to flying schools.
And the Royal Air Force are not operating any?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Not operating any.
In Saskatchewan.
Following the question put by the hon. member for Calgary West, did I understand the minister to say that he was going to enlarge upon the requirements essential for the development of the fields?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No. I should say to the committee that at the present time all requirements, so far as aerodromes for the empire training plan are concerned, are complete. All aerodromes have been selected. What will happen in the future, and whether this plan will be extended, is another question. At the present time, however, there is no use in bringing in any delegations, because I will tell them that we have all the aerodromes we want. Committee members will please take notice; tell them to stay home, because they will only waste their time.
I was not suggesting that, at all.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I was not referring to my hon. friend; I was speaking for his colleagues.
Do I understand that during the coming year there will be no further development of air. fields in western Canada, even on our own programme?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
All sites have been selected for the air training plan. There are a certain
War Appropriation Bill

number of elementary schools, a certain number of surface training centres, and a certain number of bombing and gunnery schools not yet developed or constituted. Each one of the sites of these schools has now been selected for the air training plan. If it so happens that the plan needs to be expanded or further developed or some other circumstance arises, other aerodromes and other sites may be selected. Meanwhile, against the time when that kind of thing may happen, the Department of Transport is surve3'ing every possible site in Canada. They have a list of them; should we ever require any more, we will go to the Department of Transport and they will tell us where to locate them.
The minister would not care to enlarge upon the requirements or the essentials which are taken into consideration in the selection of these various fields?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There is the question of water and the question of proximity to communications, railroads and that kind of thing. The question of water is perhaps the most serious we have had to face. It seems extraordinary that in a country like Canada with its lakes and rivers we cannot get sufficient water. We have had people looking for water everywhere. There is hardly a school which has been opened where there has not been trouble in getting water to it. I never for one moment imagined that this country was so dry as it has turned out to be.

I should like to ask a question of the minister in his dual caoacity as acting Minister of Pensions and National Health and Minister of National Defence for Air. No doubt there is a considerable civilian personnel in these flying schools. Perhaps the minister could tell us what percentage there is. I thought it might be possible to absorb many of these men who have been discharged from the army into the personnel, not only of the flying schools but of some of the thirty-day training camps. This might be one way to take up the slack for these fellows who have been discharged.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There would be no objection at all provided they are qualified. I understand the rule in the Department of National Defence is that no one is sent back from overseas unless he is in category E, and a man in that category is not fit for an3'thing like hard work. Those who were placed in category C were kept on as line communication troops as long as they could do anything. I would have no objection to taking on exsoldiers; as a matter of fact, they have preference in our department for positions round the camps.
If a man is in category E, is he entitled to a pension?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Not always; he might be in category E because of disabilities not due to service.
If they were due to service?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: He should get a pension. Probably he would be hospitalized in Canada for some little time.

The minister has not yet answered the question which led up to this interesting discussion. A 3-ear ago the minister made it quite clear that representations by boards of trade and such organizations would not influence the department in choosing sites. I notice from the press that delegations are still coming to Ottawa to try to persuade the government to decide on such and such a site. I should like the minister to make it clear whether such representations are of any use, or whether, if certain constituencies bad elected as members of parliament those of other political stripes, they would have been more successful in getting air training centres.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I made a trip west last
summer, and it was made quite miserable by delegations that waited on me every time the train stopped. I told them that there was no use bothering me; that if they wanted to make representations, they should make them to the Department of Transport or to the officers of my department. I told them that if they wanted to fill reams of paper or make books of plans and so on, it would do no good to present them to me; they should be sent to the officers of the department who would make the decision.
But they did not believe you.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No. I had a delegation here last week, and I simply told them that they had wasted their time and money, that they might as well go home. They wanted to know if I could tell them if they had a chance of further development, and I told them, "I do not know and I do not care." I am sorry to say that the delegations do not like me any more, but that is the only way to handle them.

There is an
observers' school at Malton, but on wet days the young fellows there can do nothing but lie in their bunks. They have no recreation hall, and I do not suppose it would cost much to erect one.

War. Appropriation Bill

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am not sure whether a recreation hall goes with an air observers' school.

May I intervene to say that we have a fine recreation hall in the village of Malton. A community spirit has developed, and they are taking care of most of the young men in both the elementary training school and the observers' school. We will be ready to welcome the hon. member for St. Paul's in the recreation rooms at any time.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Then I do not need to
build one?
No, not at the moment.
What is the position with respect to the Gander airport?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The work progressed rather slowly at first on account of illness and difficulty in getting materials.
What about the labour situation?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Newfoundland labour is perhaps not as accustomed to working steadily over long periods of time as is labour in this part of the country. They do like to get away for Christmas. Then measles broke out, and there were 101 difficulties in the way of making rapid progress. I saw the contractor this week, and he reports that since about the middle of January things have been progressing much more rapidly. As a matter of fact, the original contract has been about completed. There have been some complaints which, as my hon. friend knows, were well founded.
Has there been any relaxation on the part of the Newfoundland government with respect to letting in skilled and ordinary labour?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The contractor told me that he did not anticipate much trouble in that regard. He has seen the United States authorities who are expending large sums of money in Newfoundland; he was also in communication with Mr. Wood, commissioner of works, who is also in charge of the department of 14873-103
labour in Newfoundland, and he tells me that arrangements with regard to labour have been worked out to his satisfaction. He believes that no further difficulties will ensue. It may be necessary for him to bring key men from Canada.
How much more development is proposed at that point?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I should not like to say offhand. It is rather complicated.

Can the minister give us some information with respect to conditions at Mossbank, Saskatchewan, where the water supply has been bad and there has been a great deal of difficulty? There was a rumour there that conditions were so bad that the department was considering closing up the school.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We do not close any schools. For better or worse we go through with them; but, as my hon. friend knows, there was some little difficulty with a crew of about sixteen men who went to Dafoe and ran into a snowstorm. The buildings which we had for their accommodation had not been heated at that time, but I understand that difficulty was ironed out. That was at Dafoe, not Mossbank. I have no information here about Mossbank. .
Has the water supply been taken care of? I understand that it comes in under contract by truck at the present time.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall be glad to look into that.

I did not want to poach on the preserves of the hon. member for Peel when I said that I had been at Malton, but there were two or three of my constituents in Malton whom I wanted to meet, and I found conditions as I have stated. The boys only had their bunks to go to on wet days, and so on. I know that my hon. friend has been instrumental in having a wonderful hall put up at Malton, and we are very proud of it, but it is two and a half miles for the men to walk to from the preliminary school. I thought I would just bring the matter to the attention of the minister because I knew he would take care of it.
Are all air observer schools in Canada operated by private companies?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

Is there a standard form of agreement covering the operation of the schools?

War Appropriation Bill

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes; I have produced it in the house two or three times and I shall be glad to do so again. Both elementary and observer schools are civilian schools. Alay I say with respect to civilian schools generally that there has been a good deal of criticism as to the profits being made, and I had intended referring this whole question of civilian school contracts to the war expenditures committee. I wanted to do so before it became a matter of political controversy, before hon. gentlemen opposite would have to attack the system and before I would have to defend it. Up to the present it has not been a matter of controversy. The whole thing is a matter of judgment.
So far as the elementary schools are concerned, they are all sponsored by flying clubs, and I do not think there will ever be the slightest difficulty about them because most of them are turning their profits back to the government in one way or another. I think that could be readily shown, and I would have been more than pleased to have these men come before the committee and explain their case. .
There are, however, some instances in which perhaps rather large profits may be made, and in view of the fact that it would take too long to get the matter before the committee I am now going into that to see what can be done by voluntary action on the part of the clubs themselves.
With regard to the air observer schools, the same condition obtains, I think, and I am having that looked into. I can assure the committee that if there are any profits that look a little bit high, they will be cut down by agreement between the government and the operators.

I did not know that the same principle applied to the observer schools as applies to the elementary schools. We not only guarantee against any loss but guarantee a profit of 5 per cent, which is pretty profitable to-day having regard to profits available in other lines. What was the inception of the system? How did that arise? Was it at the instance of the government or of the flying schools themselves?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
They have civilian schools in England, and the general outlines of the plan came from England. So far as Canada was concerned, we have here a large number of flying clubs, all of which wanted to do their bit. The gentlemen in charge were reputable. These flying clubs were spread all across the country and they all wanted to do their bit. These gentlemen came here; we had a meeting of the flying clubs, and they drew up a tentative agreement. At that time Major

Seymour, a barrister of St. Catharines, represented the flying clubs, and Mr. K. S. Mac-lachlan, then deputy minister for air, and Mr. Henry Borden, represented the government in drawing up this agreement. None of them had any very great experience in how the thing would work out, so it may be a loosely drawn agreement in certain respects.
The reason why I think the arrangement was a good one is that it enabled us to get experienced management we would not have been able to obtain otherwise. We got the experienced management of these different schools, something we did not- have in the air force. We did not have a sufficient number of men accustomed to run such schools, so it was necessary to bring in civilians with some experience and of some business acumen to run these schools. Whether, after another six months or a year, we shall require to continue operating them as civilian schools, I couldi not be sure, but it was a godsend to us that we had in Canada at that time a number of people, commercial companies, bush pilots, bush operators, and flying clubs, who knew how to put planes in the air, maintain them in the air and keep them operating. That is something we have to be grateful for. I do not think there is the slightest doubt that the contract can be modified and amended in such a way that the profits will be even less than reasonable because these people have met us so far at every turn.

I have had a good many representations made to me about this matter, but I have never raised the question. One thing that was represented to me was that all these flying schools were not being treated alike, and that some were really eliminated. Is there anything in that charge?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I think I can say that every flying club in Canada that was operating-I am speaking of flying clubs now; these are the amateurs, not the commercial corporations- has had an elementary flying school. I do not know of one that has not, and I have not heard of any complaints from them. In some instances, in fact, we have been obliged to amalgamate them; that is, to get clubs at a long distance to come in to other places w'here the schools were being operated. Chatham, for example, is being operated by the Moncton flying club.
With regard to the commercial companies, I am not sure that every commercial company has had an opportunity-
I think that is the trouble.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
One difficulty there is that a great many of these commercial companies

Tl'fir Appropriation Bill
are affiliated in one way or another, either by stock control or by directorates, with a fairly large corporation, and while one company carrying on under a certain name may perhaps claim that it has not had an opportunity, the parent company, with which it is affiliated may have probably had an opportunity in two or three different places.
How many new private schools have been started?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I do not know just what
my hon. friend means by "new." We have seventeen elementary flying schools, all operated by civilians, and six air observer schools, all operated by civilians.

How many of these
were in operation at the time the scheme was introduced?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
This is all part of the
scheme. The flying clubs were being operated as flying clubs. They had nothing to do with the empire training plan. They were simply organizations of people interested in flying in their locality, and they called themselves flying clubs. I am under the impression that the Department of National Defence gave them a subsidy at one time. I am not sure whether that was cut out afterwards. In any event, they have started to operate schools only since last April.
Does the minister exercise any control over the salaries paid in these several schools, in order to ensure uniformity throughout the dominion?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
No. The salaries paid in
the schools are a matter for the provincial departments of labour, which really decide what are the prevailing rates and what are the salaries paid in the civilian schools. I understand my hon. friend is referring to civilian schools?

I refer particularly
to those holding executive, managerial, secretarial, positions and the like.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We give a flat rate. The
contract calls for a flat payment of $1,400 a month covering manager-I am not quite sure of that-telephone operators, stenographers and all the rest of the staff. We give them that flat rate and they are supposed to pay their people out of it. I believe some of them make a little profit. I would have to check that. Of course we take 75 per cent of the profit away.

Well, 30
per cent anyway.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

speechtext: Are they not guaranteed 5 per cent on their investment?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I am not quite sure. I
think they are guaranteed. I have not looked at the contract for some time.
Are the instructors in those elementary training schools and the like, subject to overseas service?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Originally the instructors were engaged by these schools, and they employed whom they wanted to. They went out and hired bush pilots, or Americans, and paid them whatever they thought was the right salary. As time went on, they had more difficulty in finding them, so they came to us; what we did was that we trained them and turned them out as sergeants on leave without pay, and the flying schools pay them their salaries. Under these circumstances, of course, we can call them back at any time, because they belong to the Royal Canadian Air Force, and we can send them overseas if necessary.
And there is military supervision of these flying schools?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There is a supervisor, a Royal Air Force officer, who supervises the curriculum of flying and generally acts, so to speak, as the school principal. The civilian manager looks after the maintenance of the aircraft, the messing and so forth.

I understand that there
is a training school at Goderich, Ontario, and that last summer they were selling stock up in the county prior to the starting of the school. Would the minister explain the set-up?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
An elementary school was originally required to raise $35,000 in order to show its good faith. In most instances that amount was pretty rapidly raised, especially for the larger cities. Around Goderich and Huron counties, what I believe is called the Huron-Goderich club went out and sold stock, I understand in amounts of S100 or $200. to the farmers. I do not think it was sold to them as a money-making proposition; I believe they are not going to make money, because there will not be very much profit out of it. They wanted to get as many people as possible
War Appropriation Bill

interested in the enterprise. In most other cities half a dozen people subscribed five or ten thousand dollars and let it go at that. But interest has been much more widely distributed in connection with the Goderich school than any other school I know of.

What control wiil the
people of the county have?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know in whose hands the control of the stock lies; I do not know where the majority of the stock is. If the majority are farmers from Huron county, I suppose they could get together and oust the manager and carry on if they so desire; but if it is a matter of getting more profits, they will have to come to us, and I will not give them any.
The government provide the buildings and the plant?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The buildings, aircraft and everything else.
All the plant?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

If the
committee is through with the discussion on aeroplanes, I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services if he will make a statement to the committee, and I would like him to explain the basis upon which a large number of United States privately-owned yachts were bought in the early stages of the war and brought into Canada, the purposes for which they were bought, and what use is being made of them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: This matter of the yachts is rather an unusyal arrangement which happened before I came to Ottawa. I am familiar with it, but I do not know whether even now, after a year, it would be wise to announce publicly the form in which that transaction was made. 1 would be glad to tell my hon. friend.
I will forgive the hon. gentleman if he will not tell the form, because I know it. I should, however, like to know how many we bought, how many are in use now, and for what purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
forget whether it is fifteen or sixteen. They are all in use.
For what purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Well, for war purposes.

All right- if that is all the minister wants to tell.
TMr. Power.]

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They are in use in different parts of the world. I do not know if I should say exactly where they are. All the yachts have been armed. They are patrolling the various waters in which they have been placed, and are carrying on the regular duties of ships of that class. I do not know that I can say much more than that.
Of course that is quite illuminating! Have any been used for living quarters or office quarters for members of the naval staff?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, none of those.
Some ships which have been requisitioned have been so used, have they not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not for the Canadian staff. There is one ship in Halifax used by a flag officer commanding there, the British representative and his staff. That is the only yacht I know of which is used for living accommodations of any naval officer.

We did
not get very far on that.

I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence if his department has authorized deductions from the pay of men in the reserve army to set up regimental funds. I have heard a number of instances of it. I have never actually known of a case, except one which came to me the other day, of a certain regiment in the west, in which it was announced that authorization had been given by which each man was to have deducted from his pay-I believe it was S9; I can check the memo on it-to go towards the regimental fund. I was wondering whether the minister knew anything of that, and whether it was authorized.

I have not heard of it, and have no idea of anything of that kind being done. If my hon. friend would give me the name of the unit, either privately or at the present time, I shall be happy to look into the matter.

I shall be very glad to give it to the minister. I can quite understand why it is done. I am not speaking in a spirit of criticism, because I think I know something of the problem the men are up against in the reserve units, but there is a feeling among many of the men that there is a difficult problem. I know the minister is familiar with it because he has had a good

War Appropriation Bill
deal of experience along that line. No allowance is made for buying things like multigraph machines and other equipment they must have if they are to operate a unit properly. The result is that they are usually forced to do one of two things. Either they have to use money from the canteen fund, or they make a whip-around among the officers and non-commissioned officers. In this particular case, I am informed, they actually deducted so much from each man's pay. If they did, I am not complaining about the act as about the necessity for such a thing. Some allowance should be made for reserve army units whereby they will have funds to buy the type of thing they need in order to keep the regiment working smoothly.

Mv hon. friend has mentioned multigraph machines. That is not quite in keeping with an officers mess. The things about an officers mess that I think of are dishes, cutlery, furniture and such necessities. Is he advocating the other as well?
No.

My colleague has mentioned a headache. He does not know about headaches until he has to deal with allowances for such matters. My hon. friend is referring to provision for equipment for company offices and battalion headquarters?

Yes. I am not thinking of officers messes. That is something they can take care of; but it is too much to ask these men, the rank and file, to contribute to office equipment which is not provided for by the department.
My hon. friend suggested that a deduction was made not only from officers but from the rank and file.

Exactly; and as a matter of fact, indirectly, in practically all units it is taken from the rank and file, because it is taken from the canteen fund and that comes from the men who buy cigarettes and chocolate bars from the canteen. Therefore, indirectly all ranks contribute to buy the things that should be a responsibility of the department.

The Minister of National Defence for Naval Services is reticent on the question of these yachts. I am not suggesting that there is anything to hide. He might have given a little more information than he did. He is not going to get into trouble over this matter. The position is entirely changed since that transaction took place about a year ago.
Since Saturday night.

Yes, or last Wednesday, I assume, would be the better date upon which to base the change. If he is not willing to give more information, I shall not press him, because doubtless he has what seems to him to be good and sufficient reasons for not conveying any information. I think it might have been better if, at the time this transaction was put through, a little more information had been given the public by the government, because many unjust statements were made by people who did not understand the position and who thought some people were getting something for nothing. I understood it from the beginning. I never raised the question in this house before to-night. I thought that now we might be told the story,, but if that is not possible, I shall not press it.

I handled the transactions and perhaps I can give my hon. friend certain assurances. They were purchased through the Department of Munitions and Supply or its predecessor board. We carried out the transaction in accordance with the laws of the United States government, and to do that we had to get several individuals each to buy a yacht. Those individuals were carefully chosen as men who knew yachts, men outstanding in the community, who were willing to volunteer to give time without profit.
I am not questioning all that. I want to know how much was spent.
It was not large, altogether not more than a million and a half.
For how many ships?
Fifteen.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Fourteen.
And they are all in commission?
Yes, and at the time, of course, they were needed. Patrol vessels were badly needed, and these could be got and armed quickly.
They were in commission for the most part?
Yes. They were valuable.
I never criticized it.

I want to make it clear that these men arranged their own financing privately. At the end of the transaction the men received their absolute out-of-pocket expenses. No one made five cents profit on
War Appropriation Bill

the boats. As a matter of fact, the men went to a great deal of trouble to perform the service, and I was able to call them together and thank them for a really patriotic service.

I am
delighted to hear the minister's statement, because I will tell him that in eastern Canada there was a great deal of misapprehension about that transaction, and a very unjust inference was drawn, perhaps from the secrecy with which the thing was carried on. I understand thoroughly the reason why it was done in that way; it was because of the laws of a certain foreign country. It had to be carefully examined and carried out. But I had numerous letters last session with regard to this matter, that so-and-so, and so-and-so had got a private yacht and unloaded it on the government. I never for a moment believed that there was anything of the sort, knowing some of the men at least who allowed their good offices to be used in connection with that service. It seems to me the statement the minister has made to-night is a little bit of belated justice to these men, having regard to the uninformed criticism which was made of the transaction. As far as I am concerned I welcome this statement; and as far as I am further concerned the transaction is closed.
I should, however, like to have from the minister a statement of the policy of his department in connection with expenditures of a very substantial sum with respect to the acquisition of vessels during the past fiscal year, or the one now closing, the break-down of which he gave the other day and for which we have had no explanation, and also with respect to the coming year, so far as the acquisition of vessels is concerned; what has been done, and what is proposed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall be glad to give the statement. I cannot give details at this moment, but, generally speaking, there are only two ways of acquiring the vessels needed. We have either to build the vessel or to buy it. There is also a third way, and that is to charter the vessel. It depends on the purpose for which the vessel is required which method will be followed. In the case of United States yachts, the quickest way to get ships of that class into commission in the Canadian navy was to obtain them in the way in which they were obtained, and that practice was followed. Certain steps had to be taken, and I do not think, even at this time, while conditions have changed, we should go back and say that a year ago certain things were done in a manner which at that time might be open to criticism.
[Mr. Howe.l
I do not think it was open to criticism, but it was open to misconception because of lack of knowledge. I would rather put it that way, that there was misconception.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Could anyone tell the Canadian people at that time what was done?
I did not say they could.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It could not possibly be told.

The time has arrived when it has been done, and I welcome it as clearing up certain misapprehensions which were created by the methods adopted. What I ask now is: What is the minister going to do with the vote of $56,000,000, mentioned on page 1495 of Hansard, for the acquisition and construction of vessels? I further ask him what he did with the money, $28,525,000 in the last fiscal year or up to January 31, 1941. I think we are entitled to that information.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall be glad to give my hon. friend an analysis of those two figures, the amount for the current year and the amount asked for the coming year, as to ships to be constructed for us, ships to be bought and ships to be chartered.
The minister cannot give it to-night?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not think I can give the exact figures. I have the detail here, but I think I can arrange it in shorter form by to-morrow.
I am quite willing to let it wait until to-morrow.

Has the Minister of National Defence had opportunity during the recess to find the answer to the question which I put some time before six o'clock with regard to various medical categories in the reserve army?
No, I have not. I will have it to-morrow.

I wish to ask a question of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. Some time ago the people of Canada were delighted to hear that in the army promotion would be made from the ranks. I have heard some criticism of the way in which promotions are made in the navy. Could the minister outline to the committee how promotions are made?

War Appropriation Bill

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Some promotions are made from the ranks. I think an announcement to that effect was made before Christmas. Generally speaking, if a man wants to take a commission in the Royal Canadian Navy he would enter the navy as a cadet and, undergo a course of training in the naval college in England for a period of two years, after which he would serve some time on ships and receive his commission. The more common course to pursue is for a man desiring to be an officer to join the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve, one of the eighteen divisions of that reserve found in the leading cities of Canada from Charlottetown to Vancouver. He joins as a sort of probationer and is observed by the officers commanding, and if he seems suitable for commissioned rank in the navy he is given a course. If he passes that course satisfactorily, he is sent to sea. Of the men training on the west coast now, a certain number have been taken from the ranks, I forget the exact number; but a certain number have been taken from what is called the lower deck, that is men in the ranks, and they are training along with others for positions at this time.
Could the minister give at some other time the figures for the number taken from the ranks?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes; I should not like to give a figure now; I am not sure what it is.

Is	there a minimum
educational requirement for cadets?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, there is an educational requirement for an officer in the navy; he has to be able to do certain things with instruments which require a certain amount of mathematical training. It is all laid down in the regulations. It is, I think, about equivalent of matriculation.

I wish to ask a question of the Minister of National Defence. On page 1352 of Hansard where the appropriation for this department is broken down, I see an item of $8,232,697 for internment operations. Could the minister give details of this item? It seems a large amount. What proportion is recoverable from the Ignited Kingdom?

I do not want to shift responsibility, but the matter of recovery from the United Kingdom is in the hands of the Minister of Finance. Only lately I think an agreement has been concluded with regard to internment camps. It was under discussion
for a long time, and certain proposals were made. Internment camps are, however, under the Department of the Secretary of State, although the Department of National Defence does the work. We supply the guards and do the running and administration.
Do you select the sites?

Generally speaking, the sites are selected by the director of internment operations who is appointed upon the recommendation of the Secretary of State but who has close liaison with the Department of National Defence. I think the sites are selected by him in consultation with the officers commanding in the different districts. I will try to give such break-down as I can. What has my hon. friend in mind, pay and allowances for instance?
It seems quite a large item.

I have another question to ask of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. There was some criticism on the Pacific coast when the captured German ship the Weser was refitted and a crew was taken from the Atlantic coast to man the ship. The seamen in Vancouver claim that there are many idle sailors there who could have done the work just as well. What explanation has the minister on that point?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
have nothing to do with that.

That boat was condemned and turned over to the Canadian government merchant marine, and a crew was sent out by the Canadian government merchant marine. I presume it was a crew they had immediately available in the east, and instead of recruiting one in the west they sent out a crew they had available from another boat. I think it was not a complete complement of officers and men; I think it was only officers they sent out. I have a dossier on that boat, but I do not have it before me. I will try to get the information.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury); What has the minister to say about the Vancouver Sun's story on that boat?

I have been expecting a question on that. I have a complete story, I have it well briefed but I do not have it here.
Progress reported.
